notes: Species templates (real organisms or groups). firstAge/lastAge are GeologicalAge names; empty lastAge = still alive today. Sizes are typical adult body lengths.

species.description: A tiny gliding flagellate of mud and soil that slides along on its long trailing flagellum, feeling the way with a short one sheathed in a stiff snout, and eats bacteria. Apusomonads are the closest single-celled relatives of the branch that holds the amoebae, the fungi and the animals, the Amorphea, and stand here for its ancestor, over a billion years old: a small, bacteria-eating cell with two flagella that could also put out pseudopods.

A small predatory flagellate of seas and lakes that swims with two unequal flagella and swallows bacteria and smaller flagellates whole. Telonemids are a deep branch of their own, next to the great group of the ciliates, foraminifera, diatoms and brown algae, the SAR, within the Diaphoretickes, which also holds the red and green algae and the plants. It stands here for the ancestor of that whole branch, over a billion years old.

A tiny freshwater flagellate that beats a long flagellum inside a deep groove along its underside, sweeping bacteria into it to eat. This feeding groove gave the excavates their name, a scattered set of flagellates that includes the euglenids and trypanosomes and the gut parasites without mitochondria. Malawimonads may sit near the very root of the eukaryote tree, and stand here for the ancestor of the excavates, well over a billion years old.

A flat, ribbed oval, usually a few centimetres to about 20 cm long (the giant 1.4 m specimens are usually placed in Dickinsonia rex), that grazed microbial mats; fat molecules in its fossils show it was an animal.
A broad, quilted Ediacaran animal that left trails of feeding marks on the mats.
A small segmented animal with a horseshoe-shaped head, once thought to be an early arthropod.
A slug-like animal that scraped microbial mats with a toothed proboscis; perhaps an early relative of molluscs.
A grain-sized burrower, one of the earliest known bilaterian animals, with a front, a back and a gut.
A deep-sea frond anchored by a disc; the first Precambrian fossil recognised, found in Charnwood Forest.
A disc with three curved arms: a body plan found in no living animal.
Stacked cone-in-cone tubes: one of the first animals with a mineral skeleton and the first reef builder.
Armored marine arthropods with compound eyes; one of the most successful animal groups, surviving almost 300 million years until the end-Permian extinction.
A Cambrian apex predator from the Burgess Shale: a stem-group arthropod with grasping frontal appendages and large compound eyes.

Five-eyed Burgess Shale animal with a long flexible proboscis ending in a grasping claw, used to pass food back to a mouth under its head. It swam with rows of overlapping lateral flaps bearing gills and steered with a fan-shaped tail; when it was first presented in 1972 the audience reportedly laughed at the reconstruction.

A small spiny worm on stilt-like clawed legs, related to modern velvet worms, with seven pairs of protective spines along its back. It was famously first reconstructed upside down and back to front, with the spines taken for legs; its small head with simple eyes and a ring of teeth was only identified in 2015.
An early chordate with a notochord and zig-zag muscle blocks, related to the ancestors of all vertebrates.
One of the earliest known vertebrates, from the Chengjiang biota of China: a tiny jawless fish with eyes and a skull of cartilage.

A giant straight-shelled endocerid nautiloid, among the largest animals of the Ordovician seas: its thick conch probably reached several metres, though the biggest claims are debated. A huge siphuncle along the belly, partly filled with cone-shaped deposits, probably acted as ballast that let the shell hang level in the water. It was probably a slow ambush predator of trilobites and other animals near the sea floor.

A single-celled freshwater predator about 50 micrometres across: a foamy, vacuolated sphere bristling with stiff radiating axopodia that snare passing flagellates and ciliates. Heliozoans leave no fossils, so it stands in for the ancient protist plankton that every later food web rests on.

A slipper-shaped ciliate about a quarter of a millimetre long, rowing through ponds on thousands of beating cilia and sweeping bacteria into its oral groove. Like most protists it leaves no fossils; it stands in for the ancient freshwater plankton.

A shapeless single cell that crawls by flowing into finger-like pseudopods and engulfs bacteria, algae and smaller protists whole. Soft-bodied amoebae leave almost no fossil record, so it stands in for the ancient protists of every age.

A rosette of a dozen single cells that divided without letting go, each beating a long flagellum inside a collar of fine microvilli that strains out bacteria. Choanoflagellates are the closest living relatives of animals: their collar cells are almost identical to those that line sponges, and colonies like this one hint at how the first animals came together from single cells.

A long, worm-like single cell about a fifth of a millimetre long that lives in the gut of marine worms, holding on to the gut wall by a small pointed tip and swaying and coiling in the gut contents, whose nutrients it soaks up through its pleated surface. It is an archigregarine, the simplest of the sporozoans: the class of single-celled parasites that also includes the malaria parasite, which lost the ability to live on their own and spread from host to host as tough-walled spores. Sporozoans are among the oldest parasites of animals, and were probably living in worms on the Ediacaran seafloor.

An amoeba that lives inside a shell it builds itself: a brown, hat-shaped test of protein plates, open underneath by a round hole through which it puts out a few blunt pseudopods to crawl over pond mud and moss and to engulf algae and bacteria. Small vase-shaped shells of testate amoebae in rocks some 750 million years old are among the oldest fossils of any eukaryote that can be named, so shelled amoebae were already living before the Ediacaran began.

A soil and pond amoeba that is not an amoebozoan at all but belongs to the excavates, far from the true amoebae: it crawls by bursting out one broad rounded pseudopod after another and eats bacteria. When its water changes it can grow two flagella and swim off within minutes, then turn back into an amoeba, or wall itself up in a cyst to wait out drying. It shows how often the amoeboid way of life evolved in different branches of the eukaryotes.

A spindle-shaped green flagellate of ponds and puddles that swims with one long whip and steers toward light with a red eyespot. It has chloroplasts, captured long ago from a green alga, and makes its food by photosynthesis, but in the dark it lives on dissolved food like an animal, which is why it was claimed both by botanists and zoologists. Its flexible skin of spiral protein strips lets it squirm and change shape.

A foraminifer whose shell is a single undivided tube of cemented sand grains, coiled flat like a rope. From the open end it spreads a web of fine sticky threads of cytoplasm over the seafloor to catch bacteria, algae and organic particles. Simple tubular, sand-built shells like this are the oldest foraminifera in the fossil record, from the early Cambrian, and Ammodiscus-like forms have lived on ever since.

One of the oldest known radiolarians, from the middle Cambrian of Australia: a drifting single cell with a spherical lattice shell of glass (silica) bristling with long radial spines. Along the spines it spread threads of cytoplasm to catch smaller plankton. Radiolarian skeletons, sinking for half a billion years, have built up thick layers of siliceous ooze and chert on the ocean floor.

A social amoeba of forest soil and leaf litter. Its cells live alone, eating bacteria, until food runs out; then tens of thousands stream together, called by pulses of a chemical signal, into a slug that crawls toward light and heat. The slug rises into a fruiting body: a fifth of the cells die to build a stalk, lifting the rest as a ball of spores to be carried away. Its cooperation, and its cheaters, make it a model of how multicellular life could arise.

A many-headed slime mould: a single giant cell with millions of nuclei that spreads as a bright yellow network of veins over rotting logs and leaves of damp forests, eating bacteria, fungi and decaying matter. Its cytoplasm sloshes back and forth through the veins every minute or two, and the network thickens the paths that lead to food, so well that it can find the shortest route through a maze. When it dries out it hardens into a resting crust.

A giant among dinoflagellates, up to two millimetres across: a buoyant, balloon-like cell that floats at the sea surface and catches plankton and diatoms with a single sticky tentacle. When the water is disturbed it flashes blue, so its blooms make breaking waves and boat wakes glow at night; by day the same blooms can turn the sea pink or red. Dinoflagellate cysts are common fossils from the Triassic on.

A giant foraminifer of the warm Eocene seas, a single cell building a coin-shaped limestone shell several centimetres across with hundreds of chambers in a tight spiral. It lived on sunlit sea floors with algae in its shell that fed it by photosynthesis. Its shells make up whole beds of limestone: the stone of the pyramids of Giza is full of them, and the Greek historian Herodotus took them for the petrified lentils of the builders' rations.

A planktonic foraminifer drifting in cool surface waters, its small chalky shell of four swollen chambers bristling with long fine spines that hold out a web of cytoplasm for catching food. When they die, the shells of Globigerina and its kin rain down and cover vast areas of the deep ocean floor as globigerina ooze; the oxygen in them records the temperature of the seas they lived in, which makes them a key to past climates.

A parasitic amoeba of the gut of humans and other primates, spread as hardy cysts in water and food tainted with faeces. Most infections cause no harm, but sometimes it invades the gut wall, kills the host's cells and swallows red blood cells, causing amoebic dysentery. Like its free-living relatives among the archamoebae, it has lost its mitochondria, keeping only tiny remnants of them, and lives without oxygen.

A slender, corkscrewing flagellate that lives in the blood of African mammals and is carried from one to the next by the bite of tsetse flies. It swims with a flagellum running along a frilly undulating membrane, and escapes the host's immune defences by changing its coat of surface proteins again and again. In people and cattle it causes sleeping sickness and nagana; wild antelopes and other game mostly carry it unharmed.

A pear-shaped flagellate of the small intestine of mammals that clings to the gut lining with a sucking disc on its underside. Its two nuclei and the bodies below them make it look like a face peering down a microscope. It swims with four pairs of flagella and spreads as cysts in drinking water, causing diarrhoea, beaver fever, in people and animals. It has no proper mitochondria and was once thought to be a living relic of the first eukaryotes.

A pear-shaped flagellate of the mouth and throat of birds, spread by pigeons and doves through the milk they feed their chicks and through shared drinking water, and caught by the hawks and falcons that eat them. It swims with four flagella at the front and a fifth along an undulating membrane, and has a stiff rod, the axostyle, sticking out behind. In finches and other songbirds it can cause deadly throat sores.

The deadliest malaria parasite, a sporozoan that lives inside the red blood cells of people and multiplies there, bursting them in waves of fever. Its life alternates between humans and Anopheles mosquitoes, which pick up its crescent-shaped sexual stages with a meal of blood and pass it on with their next bite. It descends from a parasite of gorillas, which crossed over to humans in Africa, and has shaped human history and even the human genome.

Not one animal but a colony of specialised zooids: a gas-filled float that sails on the wind, trailing stinging tentacles many metres long that paralyse fish. Siphonophores are soft-bodied and essentially absent from the fossil record; their cnidarian relatives go back to the Cambrian.

An egg-laying mammal from eastern Australia that hunts river invertebrates with eyes and ears shut, finding prey through electroreceptors in its rubbery bill. Males carry a venomous ankle spur. The living species is known from the Pleistocene; platypus relatives date back to the Cretaceous.

The bird with the longest wingspan alive, over three metres. It can glide for hours over the Southern Ocean without flapping, feeding on squid and fish, and returns to sub-Antarctic islands to raise a single chick every two years.

A bear from the mountain forests of central China that lives almost entirely on bamboo, eating for half the day and gripping stems with a thumb-like wrist bone. Its lineage reaches back into the Miocene; the living species appears in the Pleistocene.

Slender flies whose larvae filter-feed in still water while the adults sip nectar; only females take blood, to fuel their eggs. The oldest known mosquitoes are preserved in Cretaceous amber about 99 million years old.

One of the earliest trilobites, from the early and middle Cambrian of China and Australia: a spiny, crescent-headed scavenger and predator. Redlichia rex from South Australia grew to about 12 cm and had spiny legs for tearing up its food.

A large golden orb-weaver from East Asia, now spreading across the south-eastern United States. Females spin webs up to a metre across from golden silk; young spiders disperse by 'ballooning' on silk threads carried by the wind.

The largest fossil spider known, from the 165-million-year-old lake beds of Daohugou in Inner Mongolia, China. A golden orb-weaver like the living Nephila, with a body 2.5 cm long and a leg span of about 15 cm, it had long legs with tufts of hairs and probably spun large, golden webs between the horsetails and ferns, catching the insects of a world without flowers. It shows that the great orb-weavers have hardly changed in 165 million years.

A sparrow-sized bird of Eurasian rivers and lakes that watches from a low perch, then plunges headfirst into the water after small fish. Its brilliant blue is structural colour, made by light scattering in the feathers rather than by pigment.

A long-legged shorebird of western North American wetlands that sweeps its upturned bill from side to side through shallow water to catch insects and crustaceans. Its head and neck turn cinnamon in the breeding season.

A ground-dwelling songbird of south-eastern Australian forests, famous for mimicry: displaying males copy other birds, and even chainsaws and camera shutters, while fanning a lacy silver tail over their heads.

The largest living marsupial, hopping across the Australian interior at up to 60 km/h on springy tendons that recycle energy with every bound. The joey is born the size of a bean and grows for months in its mother's pouch.
A heron-like bird of forest streams in Central and South America. Finely barred and well hidden at rest, it startles predators by spreading its wings into a display of two huge 'sunburst' eyespots.

A perching duck of wooded lakes and rivers in East Asia that nests in tree holes; the ducklings leap to the ground soon after hatching. The drake's upright orange 'sails' and whiskers make it one of the most ornate ducks in the world.

The most widespread large mammal of the Americas, from Canada to Peru. When alarmed it bounds away with its tail raised, flashing the white underside as a warning to the herd. Bucks regrow their antlers every year.

The only truly social cat: prides of related females hunt together while males defend the territory. Lions ranged across Africa, Eurasia and the Americas during the Pleistocene; today they survive in sub-Saharan Africa and India's Gir Forest.

A large, adaptable monkey of African savannas and woodland that lives in troops of up to 150 with complex social ranks. It eats almost anything, from grass and fruit to insects and the occasional small antelope.

A slow, gentle grazer of warm coasts and rivers from Florida to Brazil that can eat a tenth of its body weight in seagrass a day. Sea cows are distant relatives of elephants; their lineage goes back to the Eocene.
The longest member of the weasel family, up to 1.8 m, living in noisy family groups along Amazonian rivers. Each otter's creamy throat patch is unique, and families together will chase off caimans.

A gentle giant of tropical Indo-Pacific reefs, up to 5 m across, that filters plankton by gliding with its mouth wide open and its head fins unrolled. Mantas visit 'cleaning stations' where small fish pick parasites from their skin.

One of the heaviest bony fish, over two tonnes, shaped like a swimming head with tall fins and no real tail. It eats mostly jellyfish, basks on its side at the surface to warm up, and a female can carry 300 million eggs.
A small reef fish of the Indian and Pacific Oceans that feeds almost only on coral polyps, usually in faithful pairs. The black bar through its eye hides the real eye from predators.

A striking reef fish of the Indo-Pacific with bold black, white and yellow bands, a long snout for picking sponges from crevices, and a trailing white dorsal filament. It is the only living member of its family.

One of the largest flying animals ever, with a wingspan of about 10-11 metres and the standing height of a giraffe. It probably launched itself by vaulting on its folded wings and stalked small animals on foot like a giant stork. Late Cretaceous of North America.

One of the largest land predators ever, about 12 metres long and 8 tonnes, with the strongest bite of any known land animal, strong enough to crush bone. It lived in western North America at the very end of the Cretaceous, until the asteroid impact 66 million years ago.

Termites of northern Australia's tropical savannas that build earth mounds up to 8 metres tall, among the largest structures made by any animal besides humans. Soldiers defend the colony by squirting sticky glue from a pointed snout. Termites themselves date back to the Cretaceous.

A fast-growing Indo-Pacific reef coral that spreads into broad flat tables, shading the reef below. Like all reef-building corals it lives in partnership with photosynthetic algae in its tissues, which also give it its colour. Acropora corals appear in the fossil record in the Paleogene.

A slow-growing Caribbean coral whose boulder-shaped colonies are covered in maze-like grooves, each groove lined with polyps. Large heads can be several hundred years old and help build the backbone of the reef.

A branching Caribbean coral that grows in dense antler-like thickets, sheltering huge numbers of reef fish. Broken branches can regrow into new colonies. Once dominant on Caribbean reefs, it is now critically endangered.

A North American butterfly whose caterpillars feed on milkweed and store its toxins, so the bright orange adults are poisonous to birds. Each autumn millions migrate up to 4,000 km to overwinter in the mountain forests of Mexico.

The largest shark that ever lived, perhaps 15-20 metres long, with serrated teeth the size of a hand. It hunted whales in warm seas worldwide from about 23 to 3.6 million years ago. Only its teeth and a few vertebrae fossilise, so its body shape is reconstructed from relatives.

Europe's most familiar ladybird, which can eat thousands of aphids in its lifetime. Its red-and-black colours warn predators of bitter alkaloids it oozes from its leg joints when disturbed. Adults overwinter in clusters.

A brilliantly metallic leaf beetle of East Asia that feeds on dogbane and milkweed relatives, tolerating their toxic sap. Its shining blue-green colour comes from microscopic layers in the wing cases rather than pigment.

A large European earthworm that digs vertical burrows up to two metres deep and drags fallen leaves down into them at night. Its feeding and burrowing mix and aerate the soil; Darwin called earthworms some of the most important animals in history.

A large crocodilian of the swamps and rivers of the south-eastern United States, with a broad rounded snout. Females guard their nests and carry the hatchlings in their jaws. Its genus goes back over 30 million years to the Oligocene.

A large tree-dwelling lizard of Central and South American rainforests that eats leaves and fruit. It basks high in the canopy and, when threatened, drops into the water below and swims away. A light-sensing 'third eye' on top of its head helps it spot birds of prey.

A rattlesnake of the deserts of the south-western United States and north-west Mexico whose speckled colours match the local rock, from pale granite to dark lava. Heat-sensing pits on its face let it strike warm-blooded prey in the dark.

A large sea turtle of tropical and subtropical seas, named for the green fat that its diet of seagrass and algae gives it. Females swim thousands of kilometres back to the beaches where they hatched to lay their eggs. Sea turtles first appear in the Cretaceous.

A spiny grazer of the kelp forests of North America's Pacific coast that scrapes algae with a five-toothed jaw. Where sea otters, its main predator, disappear, urchin swarms can mow kelp forests down to bare 'urchin barrens'.

A bright red-orange encrusting sponge of Caribbean reefs and mangrove roots, studded with volcano-like vents that breathe out the water it has filtered. Its tissues carry toxins that cause a burning rash on human skin, which is how it got its name. Broken fragments can regrow into new sponges.

A half-millimetre, eight-legged micro-animal that lumbers through the water films of moss, lichen and pond sediment, piercing plant cells and tiny prey with its needle-like stylets. When its home dries out it curls into a dehydrated 'tun' and can survive freezing, boiling, crushing pressure, radiation and even the vacuum of space, reviving decades later when water returns.

Not a true eel but a South American knifefish up to two metres long. Most of its body is electric organ that can discharge over 600 volts to stun prey and deter predators, while weaker pulses let it sense its murky Amazon surroundings. It gulps air at the surface, taking most of its oxygen through its mouth.

A small bat of Central and South America that feeds only on blood, mostly from livestock and other large mammals. It lands near sleeping prey, runs and hops nimbly on its thumbs and hind legs, finds a warm spot with heat sensors on its nose, and laps blood from a tiny cut kept open by anticoagulant saliva. Roost-mates that failed to feed are given a shared meal of regurgitated blood.

One of the largest flying insects ever, with a wingspan of about 70 centimetres. This griffinfly, a relative of modern dragonflies, hunted other insects over the swampy coal forests of the Late Carboniferous, about 300 million years ago. Its size was possible partly because the air then held much more oxygen than today. It is known from fossils found at Commentry, France.

A social bee living in colonies of tens of thousands of workers around a single queen. Workers gather nectar and pollen from flowers, store honey in wax combs, and use the waggle dance to tell nestmates where food is. As pollinators of crops and wild plants, they are among the most important insects to people.

A squid-like belemnite that hunted with ten hooked arms in the shallow Sundance Sea of Wyoming about 160 million years ago. Its internal guard was the chunkiest of any belemnite, about 10 cm long but 6 cm wide, and it belonged to the megateuthidids, a family thought to have mostly died out millions of years earlier.

The 'star ammonite' of the Early Jurassic seas, about 195 million years ago. Its loosely coiled shell, up to 20 cm across, has bold straight ribs and a sharp keel flanked by two grooves. Gas-filled chambers kept it buoyant while the animal hunted small prey with its arms. Its fossils are so common at Lyme Regis that a whole rock zone is named after it.

Perhaps the strangest-looking ammonite, from the Late Cretaceous seas around Japan about 90 million years ago. After a few loose spiral whorls, its shell doubled back on itself in a chain of U-bends that wrap into a knot. The pattern looks random but follows a precise growth rule that kept the animal balanced, so it could drift through the water feeding on plankton.

North America's largest land bird, with a wingspan of nearly three metres. It soars for hours on thermals over canyons and hills looking for carcasses, and raises a single chick every year or two. In the Pleistocene it fed on mammoths and other large mammals. By 1987 only 27 were left, all taken into captivity, and a breeding programme has since returned hundreds to the wild.

A huge, warty toad from Central and South America, up to 15-24 cm long. The big glands behind its eyes ooze a milky poison strong enough to kill dogs, snakes and crocodiles, and a female can lay over 30,000 eggs at once. Released in Australia in 1935 to control cane beetles, it ignored the beetles and spread across the north of the continent, becoming one of the world's most notorious invasive species.

One of the most abundant dolphins, living in fast-moving schools of hundreds or even thousands in warm and temperate seas worldwide. It is recognised by the criss-cross 'hourglass' on its flanks, tan-yellow in front and grey behind. Schools work together to herd fish and squid into tight balls, finding them by echolocation.

The most common zebra, grazing in large herds across the grasslands and savannas of eastern and southern Africa and migrating with wildebeest in search of fresh grass. Every animal's stripe pattern is unique; the stripes probably help deter biting flies. Southern populations show faint brownish "shadow stripes", and the extinct quagga was one of its half-striped subspecies.

The largest living land animal: bulls stand up to 4 metres at the shoulder and weigh around 6 tonnes. Its huge ears radiate body heat, and the trunk, a fusion of nose and upper lip with tens of thousands of muscle bundles, can pluck a single leaf or lift a log. Herds of related females and calves are led by the oldest cow, the matriarch.

A close relative of the Asian elephant, adapted to the cold mammoth steppe of the Ice Age with a shaggy double coat, a thick layer of fat, small ears and a short tail. Its long spiralling tusks could sweep snow off the grass it grazed. Most populations vanished about 10,000 years ago, but a small one survived on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago.

A giant sauropod of Late Jurassic North America, about 22 metres long and weighing perhaps 40 tonnes. Unlike most sauropods its front legs were longer than its hind legs, so its back sloped down from the shoulders and its neck rose steeply, letting it browse treetops around 9 metres up. Its skull carried a tall arch of bone over the nostrils.

The longest known predatory dinosaur, about 14 metres long, with a sail of spines up to 1.65 metres tall along its back. Its long, narrow snout and interlocking conical teeth were built for catching fish, and fossils from Morocco described in 2020 revealed a deep, paddle-like tail, suggesting it hunted in the great river systems of Cretaceous North Africa about 95 million years ago.

A massive horned dinosaur, about 8-9 metres long and up to 12 tonnes, with a solid bony frill and two brow horns up to a metre long. It cropped tough plants with a parrot-like beak and sliced them with batteries of cheek teeth. It lived in western North America in the last few million years of the Cretaceous, alongside Tyrannosaurus.

The largest armoured dinosaur, up to about 8 metres long, its low, broad back covered in a shield of bony osteoderms set into the skin. Its stiffened tail ended in a heavy bony club that could be swung into a predator's legs. It lived at the very end of the Cretaceous in western North America, alongside Tyrannosaurus and Triceratops.

Together with the bonobo, our closest living relative, sharing about 98-99% of its DNA with humans. It lives in communities of up to 150 in the forests and wooded savannas of equatorial Africa, walking on its knuckles and nesting in trees at night. Chimpanzees make and use tools, fishing termites out of mounds with stripped twigs and cracking nuts with stone hammers, and they also hunt monkeys in groups.

One of the oldest known vertebrates, about 518 million years old, from the Chengjiang biota of Yunnan, China. Only about 3 cm long and without jaws, it had a sail-like dorsal fin, a fin fold along the belly, zig-zag blocks of muscle along its body and five or six gill pouches behind the head.

A sea eagle of North American lakes, rivers and coasts, with a wingspan of up to 2.3 metres, and the national bird of the United States. It feeds mostly on fish snatched from the surface with its talons, and often steals prey from ospreys. Adults only gain the white head and tail at four or five years old. Shooting and DDT poisoning left it close to extinction in the lower 48 states by the 1960s, but it has since recovered strongly.

One of the largest flying fish, up to about 40 cm long, feeding on plankton near the surface of warm seas. To escape tuna and dolphinfish it bursts out of the water, sculls along the surface with the long lower lobe of its tail, then glides on its wing-like pectoral and pelvic fins for 100 metres or more. Juveniles carry a pair of fringed chin barbels, which give the species its name.

The largest king crab of the North Pacific's cold seas, with a spiny shell up to 28 cm across and legs spanning up to 1.8 m; its right claw is bigger than the left and the fifth pair of legs is tiny and hidden under the shell. King crabs descend from hermit crab-like ancestors rather than true crabs. Introduced to the Barents Sea by Soviet scientists in the 1960s, it has spread along the coasts of Russia and Norway.

The giraffe of Kenya and Tanzania, recognised by its jagged, vine-leaf-shaped dark patches. Bulls stand nearly 6 metres tall, the tallest of any living animal, and browse thorny acacias with a tongue up to 45 cm long. Like almost all mammals it has only seven neck vertebrae, each up to 25 cm long.

The largest and most widespread flamingo, wading in salt pans, lagoons and soda lakes from Africa and southern Europe to South Asia. It feeds with its head upside down, pumping water through its bent bill to strain out brine shrimp, insect larvae and algae. The carotenoid pigments in that food are what turn its feathers pink, and it nests in noisy colonies that can number tens of thousands of pairs.

A solitary sea anemone of rocky tide pools along the coast of California and Baja California, named for the pink-lavender rays on its green oral disc. Its stinging tentacles catch small crustaceans, fish and drifting animals, while symbiotic algae in its tissues add food from sunlight and give it its green colour. Long confused with the cloning aggregating anemone, it was only described as a separate species in 2000.

A huge land snail from East Africa whose conical shell can reach 20 cm long. Each snail is both male and female and can lay over a thousand eggs a year, and it feeds on hundreds of kinds of plants, crops and even the calcium of walls for its shell. Spread by people across the tropics, it is listed among the world's worst invasive species, and in dry weather it seals itself into its shell and waits for the rain.

A clawless spiny lobster of the reefs off Western Australia that defends itself with long, thick, spiny antennae, rasping them to make a warning sound. Burgundy with pale spots, it forages at night on molluscs, worms and algae. After moulting, pale-shelled young 'whites' migrate in great numbers to deeper water, and the species supports one of Australia's most valuable fisheries.

A slender tree frog of Central American rainforests that sleeps by day pressed flat against a leaf, its blue-and-cream flanks and orange feet tucked away so it looks all green. Disturbed, it flashes its huge scarlet eyes and bright colours to startle a predator, and sticky toe pads let it cling to the undersides of leaves. Eggs are laid on leaves over ponds, and the embryos can hatch early and drop into the water when a snake or wasp attacks the clutch.

The largest cat of the Americas, a stocky, solitary ambush hunter with the most powerful bite of any big cat for its size. Instead of a throat bite it often kills with a single bite through the skull or a turtle's shell, and it swims readily to hunt caimans, capybaras and fish. Unlike a leopard's, its rosettes usually enclose small black spots.

Also called the Norway rat, it originated on the plains of northern China and Mongolia and followed people around the world, reaching every continent except Antarctica. A female can raise five or more litters a year, and colonies dig burrow networks near water, food stores and sewers. Tame strains of it became the laboratory rat and the pet fancy rat.

One of the heaviest flying birds, weighing up to 15 kg with a wingspan that can exceed three metres. Groups fish together, swimming in a horseshoe to drive fish into the shallows and scooping them up in the stretchy throat pouch. It nests in large colonies on lakes and deltas from south-eastern Europe to Africa and Asia, and soars on thermals between feeding grounds.

A small hummingbird of cloud forest and shrubby páramo edges high in the Andes, from Venezuela to Bolivia. Males are dark bronze-green with a glittering green throat and the violet-to-coppery tail that gives the metaltails their name. Its short bill often pierces the base of long flowers to steal nectar, and on cold mountain nights it drops into torpor to save energy.

A big, long-tailed parrot of tropical forests from southern Mexico to the Amazon basin. Pairs stay together for life and fly side by side over the canopy, calling loudly, to feed on fruit, nuts and seeds, cracking hard shells with the huge hooked bill. Flocks gather at riverbank clay licks, probably for the sodium the clay contains.

A firefly of the Appalachian forests of the eastern United States, famous in the Great Smoky Mountains. For a few weeks each June the males fly at dusk flashing in bursts of five to eight pulses, then go dark together, and thousands fall into step so whole hillsides blink in unison while females answer from the ground. The larvae spend a year or two in the soil hunting snails and worms.

An armoured placoderm fish and apex predator of Late Devonian seas, about 370-360 million years ago. Instead of teeth it had self-sharpening bony jaw blades and a jointed head-and-thorax shield of thick bone plates. Only the armour fossilises well, and recent studies suggest a compact, shark-like body about 4 metres long.

One of the first four-limbed vertebrates, known from Late Devonian rocks of East Greenland about 365 million years old. It had a broad flat skull, heavy overlapping ribs that braced its chest, seven toes on each paddle-like hind foot and a fish-like tail fin. It probably lived mostly in shallow water and heaved itself across mudflats on its stout forelimbs, more like a seal than a walking lizard.

A giant sea scorpion from the Early Devonian of Germany, about 390 million years ago, and the largest arthropod known: a single 46 cm claw implies a body around 2.5 metres long. It lived in brackish and fresh water, swimming with paddle-shaped hind legs and seizing prey with huge spiny pincers. Its relatively small eyes suggest it hunted in dim or murky water.

A 375-million-year-old 'fishapod' from Arctic Canada, a transitional form between fish and four-legged animals. It had scales, gills and fins, but also a flat crocodile-like head, a mobile neck and robust front fins with wrist-like bones that could prop it up in shallow water. It probably hunted in streams and swamps, perhaps breathing air with lungs.

A roachoid, one of the early cockroach relatives that swarmed through the leaf litter of the Late Carboniferous coal forests. Like modern cockroaches it had a broad shield over its head and leathery, heavily veined forewings folded flat over its back. Roachoids were so common that their wings are among the most frequent insect fossils of the period; this species was described from the coal measures of Nova Scotia.

The largest land arthropod known, a millipede relative that grew to over two metres long and half a metre wide. It walked the open floors of Carboniferous coal forests on dozens of pairs of short legs, leaving trackways up to 50 centimetres across. It probably fed on plant matter and spores, and lived on into the earliest Permian.

A smaller species of Arthropleura, the giant Carboniferous millipede relatives, reaching perhaps 30 to 50 centimetres. It is known mainly from fragments of its armour, whose tergites carried more prominent crested ridges than those of its giant cousin. Like other arthropleurids it probably browsed plant debris on the floors of the coal swamp forests.

The earliest known reptile, a small lizard-like animal about 20 cm long from the coal forests of Nova Scotia, 312 million years ago. Its fossils were found inside the hollow stumps of giant lycopsid trees, where it may have hunted insects and millipedes. Like later reptiles it probably laid shelled eggs on land.

A giant scorpion from the Early Carboniferous, about 335 million years ago, that may have reached 70 centimetres long. It is known from East Kirkton in Scotland, where it lived among early forests around a volcanic lake. Its name means 'breathing scorpion': it was one of the first scorpions to breathe air with book lungs and hunt fully on land, probably preying on insects, other arthropods and small tetrapods.

A sail-backed predator about 3 metres long from the Early Permian red beds of Texas and Oklahoma. Despite its reptilian look it was a synapsid, more closely related to mammals than to dinosaurs, which appeared some 40 million years after it died out. Its name means 'two measures of teeth': its deep skull held small front teeth, large canine-like fangs and smaller cheek teeth, and the sail of elongated spines may have helped it warm up or served for display.

A smaller Dimetrodon, perhaps under 2 metres long, from the Early Permian of Prince Edward Island, Canada, about 290 million years ago. A farmer dug up its upper jaw in 1845, and it was named Bathygnathus borealis, 'deep jaw of the north', in 1854, one of the first sail-backed synapsid fossils ever described. A 2015 study showed it belonged to Dimetrodon. Only the deep snout with its long fangs is known, so its sail is inferred from its relatives.

A heavy, 3-metre dinocephalian from the Middle Permian of the Ural region of Russia, about 267 million years ago. Its huge skull bore bizarre bony outgrowths, tall flattened horns above the eyes and flanges on the cheeks, probably used for display or head-butting contests. Fossil skin impressions suggest smooth, glandular skin without scales or hair, and it was probably a plant-eater or omnivore.

A smaller relative of Estemmenosuchus uralensis from the same Middle Permian beds near Ocher in the Perm region of Russia, about 267 million years ago. 'Mirabilis' means 'wonderful': it had two bony horns on each side of its head, one rising from the top of the skull like a short antler and one jutting sideways from the cheek. These were probably for display or contests between rivals. Like its relative it was a bulky plant-eater or omnivore with smooth, glandular skin.

The largest carnivorous synapsid of the Permian, perhaps 5 to 6 metres long, from the Middle Permian Karoo of South Africa, about 265 million years ago. Its skull, up to 80 centimetres long, was thickened with bony bosses above the eyes and on the cheeks and bristled with big incisors and canines. Long thought to be a sluggish, semi-aquatic hunter, a 2023 study of its inner ear suggested it was agile and quick. It preyed on the big plant-eating dinocephalians around it, and vanished with them in the extinction at the end of the Middle Permian.

The largest gorgonopsian, about 3.5 metres long, and the top predator of the Late Permian of Russia, with a long, low skull and sabre-like upper canines more than 12 centimetres long. Its legs were held more upright beneath the body than those of earlier synapsids. Fossils described from South Africa in 2023 show it also reached the Karoo shortly before the end-Permian mass extinction, which it did not survive.

A larger, more robust species of Inostrancevia from the Late Permian of the Russian platform, about 254 million years ago, known from a big skull found at the same Northern Dvina locality as I. alexandri. Its name means 'broad forehead': its skull was wider across the top, with a lower, broader snout and fewer teeth. Of the many species once named in the genus, it is the only one besides I. alexandri still recognised. It was among the largest gorgonopsians, a sabre-toothed predator of the last Permian herds.

A stocky, pig-sized dicynodont that cropped plants with a horny beak and had only two teeth, a pair of tusks in the upper jaw. Its genus was one of the few large land animals to survive the end-Permian mass extinction 252 million years ago and went on to dominate Early Triassic land faunas, making up most of the vertebrate fossils in some rock layers. Its fossils in South Africa, India and Antarctica helped support the idea of continental drift.

A large chameleon of the mountain valleys and plateaus of Yemen and south-western Saudi Arabia, named for the tall helmet-like casque on its head. Its turret eyes swivel independently, and it catches insects with a sticky tongue longer than its body while gripping branches with pincer-like feet and a prehensile tail. Unusually for a chameleon it also eats leaves, which supply water in its dry home.

The largest living lizard, a monitor up to 3 metres long found only on Komodo, Rinca, Flores and a few nearby Indonesian islands. It ambushes deer, pigs and water buffalo, and venom glands in its lower jaw stop the blood from clotting so bitten prey weakens quickly. Its forked yellow tongue tastes the air and can trace carrion from several kilometres away.

A delicate pale green insect of Eurasian woodland edges, meadows and gardens, with four large net-veined wings and golden eyes. Both the adults and their bristly larvae, nicknamed aphid lions, hunt aphids and other soft-bodied insects, which makes the species a valued natural pest control in crops. Females lay each egg on top of a thin silk stalk, out of reach of their hungry siblings.

A slender straight-shelled nautiloid of the Middle Ordovician seas of Baltica, its tapering conch up to about 20 cm long, finely ringed with growth lines and divided inside into gas-filled chambers threaded by a narrow siphuncle. It hovered horizontally and hunted small prey with its arms. Its fossils, packed by the thousand into the Orthoceras limestone of Sweden and the Baltic, are among the most familiar of all cephalopod fossils.

The oldest known cephalopod, from the Late Cambrian of northeast China: a tiny, slightly curved horn-shaped shell only about a centimetre long, divided inside into very closely spaced chambers threaded by a siphuncle along its underside. Filling those chambers with gas let it lift off the sea floor and hover, the first step toward the jet-propelled nautiloids, ammonites and squid that came after it.

A small, slender, straight-shelled cephalopod of the Devonian seas, about 10 cm long, with its siphuncle running along the edge of the shell rather than through the middle. Bactritids look plain, but they were the root of two great lineages: some coiled their shells and became the ammonites, others drew the shell inside the body and gave rise to the belemnites, squid and octopuses.

A planktonic dendroid graptolite of the earliest Ordovician (long known as Dictyonema flabelliforme): a cone-shaped colony of tiny filter-feeding zooids living in tubes along many forking branches, joined by cross-links into a net and hung from a thin thread. Graptolites were hemichordates, relatives of today's tiny pterobranchs, and because it appears just above the base of the Ordovician it long served as a rough marker for the start of the period; graptolites in general are key index fossils for dating Ordovician and Silurian rocks.

A small planktonic graptolite of the Early Ordovician, shaped like a tuning fork: two slender branches hang from the founding zooid's cone, each lined with saw-toothed tubes that housed filter-feeding zooids. Graptolites were colonial hemichordates related to modern pterobranchs, and because their species changed fast and drifted across whole oceans, two-branched didymograptids like this one are key index fossils for dating Ordovician rocks.

Not a worm but the larva of a fungus gnat found only in New Zealand, living on cave ceilings and in damp, sheltered forest gullies. Each larva rests in a hammock of silk and mucus and lowers dozens of silk threads beaded with sticky droplets, then glows blue-green from the tip of its body to lure small flying insects into them. The larval stage lasts months, while the adult flies cannot feed and live only a few days. The glowworm grottos of the Waitomo Caves are famous for them.

Also called the nutria, a large semi-aquatic rodent from the rivers and marshes of southern South America, usually weighing 5 to 9 kg. Its bright orange incisors get their colour from iron in the enamel, and webbed hind feet with eyes, ears and nostrils set high on the head suit a life spent swimming. Farmed for its fur, it escaped or was released across North America, Europe and Asia, where its grazing and burrowing damage marshes and riverbanks.

One of the earliest known dinosaurs, a lightly built biped about 1 metre long from the roughly 231-million-year-old Ischigualasto Formation of north-western Argentina. Its teeth were mixed: leaf-shaped ones at the front of the upper jaw, like those of plant-eaters, and curved blades behind, so it probably ate both plants and small animals. Its hands had five fingers, three of them long and clawed for grasping. First described as an early theropod, it is now often placed near the base of the sauropodomorphs, though its exact position is still debated.

A small, slender reptile about 70 cm long from the roughly 236-million-year-old Chañares Formation of Argentina, running on long, stilt-like hind legs with a very long foot. Lagerpetids were long thought to be close to the dinosaurs; skulls and inner ears described in 2020 showed that they are the closest known relatives of the pterosaurs, so animals like it stand near the split between the flying reptiles and the dinosaurs. It probably hunted insects and other small animals.

A small lizard about 20 cm long from the 240-million-year-old rocks of the Dolomites in northern Italy, and the oldest known squamate: the group of lizards and snakes. Its name means 'big hand', for its large clawed hands. A study of its skeleton in 2018 showed that it was already a true squamate, so the ancestors of all lizards and snakes lived in the Triassic, long before the oldest known snakes. It probably hunted insects among coastal plants.

A giant ichthyosaur of the Late Triassic, about 15 metres long, with a deep, rounded body, a long narrow snout and four long, narrow flippers. Dozens of skeletons lie together in Nevada's Berlin-Ichthyosaur State Park, and it is Nevada's state fossil. Unlike later, dolphin-shaped ichthyosaurs it had only a gentle bend in its tail, and adults seem to have had few or no teeth.

An enormous ichthyosaur about 21 metres long, known from a skeleton found along the Sikanni Chief River in British Columbia, in rocks from the end of the Triassic. It was one of the largest marine reptiles ever found. Its long, slender body and long, toothless snout suggest it fed on soft prey such as squid-like animals. Described as a species of Shonisaurus in 2004, it was reassigned to Shastasaurus in 2011, though its placement is still debated.

One of the earliest mammaliaforms, a shrew-like animal about 10 centimetres long that lived from the latest Triassic into the Early Jurassic. Its sharp teeth suggest it hunted insects, and thousands of its teeth and bones have been recovered from ancient cave and fissure fillings in south Wales. Its lower jaw still had the old reptilian joint working alongside the new mammal-type joint, a step in the evolution of the mammalian middle ear.

A wolf-sized predatory cynodont of the Early and Middle Triassic, about 1.2 metres long, with a large head, powerful jaws and dog-like canines; its name means 'dog jaw'. Cynodonts like it were close relatives of the ancestors of mammals. Its fossils are found in southern Africa, South America and Antarctica, and these matching finds on now-separate continents became a classic piece of evidence for continental drift.

One of the oldest known pterosaurs, from the Late Triassic of northern Italy about 210 million years ago, with a wingspan of about one metre. Its short jaws held more than a hundred tiny teeth, many of them with three to five cusps, and fish scales found in a fossil's gut show that it caught fish. Like other early pterosaurs it had a long, stiffened tail.

A rauisuchian about 4 to 5 metres long and one of the largest predators of the Late Triassic of the south-western United States, named after the town of Post in Texas. It belonged to the crocodile line of archosaurs rather than to the dinosaurs, with a large, deep skull full of big serrated teeth and two rows of bony plates down its back. Its legs were held upright beneath the body, and its short forelimbs suggest it may sometimes have walked on its hind legs.

A raven-sized feathered dinosaur from the Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, about 150 million years old, long regarded as the oldest known bird. It combined wings of modern-looking flight feathers with toothed jaws, three clawed fingers and a long bony tail. Melanosomes preserved in a fossil feather suggest its plumage was black. Its first skeleton was found in 1861, just two years after Darwin's On the Origin of Species, and became famous evidence for evolution.

The first pterosaur to be scientifically described, named in 1809 from the Late Jurassic Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, about 150 million years old. Adults reached a wingspan of about one metre, with a long, narrow skull holding about 90 small teeth, a long neck and a very short tail. Some fossils preserve a low soft-tissue crest on the head. It probably hunted small fish and invertebrates around the lagoons of the Solnhofen islands.

A marine reptile of the Early Jurassic, about 3-3.5 metres long, with a small head on a very long neck, a broad, flat body and a short tail. It 'flew' through the water with four large, wing-like flippers, and snapped up fish and squid-like animals with its slender, pointed teeth. Its first complete skeleton was found by Mary Anning at Lyme Regis, England, and it gave its name to the whole plesiosaur group.

A pliosaur, a short-necked, big-headed plesiosaur, and one of the top predators in the seas of Jurassic Europe about 166-155 million years ago. It swam by beating four large flippers and hunted fish, cephalopods and other marine reptiles with long jaws full of big conical teeth. Fossils point to a length of about 6-7 metres; the 25-metre giant made famous by television is not supported by the bones.

A dolphin-shaped ichthyosaur about 4-6 metres long from the Jurassic seas of Europe, with a teardrop body, a crescent tail and a slender snout with small teeth. Its eyes, more than 20 cm across and supported by rings of bony plates, are among the largest relative to body size of any vertebrate, and it probably hunted squid-like prey in deep or dim water. Like other ichthyosaurs it gave birth to live young at sea.

A shrew-sized mammal, weighing perhaps 15 grams, from rocks about 160 million years old in Liaoning, north-eastern China. Described in 2011 from a nearly complete skeleton, it was proposed as the earliest known eutherian, the lineage that leads to placental mammals, which would put their split from the marsupial line in the Jurassic. Its sharp teeth suggest it ate insects, and its hand bones point to an agile climber.

A mouse-sized climber from the 125-million-year-old Yixian Formation of Liaoning, China, about 15 cm long with its tail, preserved with traces of fur. Its ankle and foot bones are those of a tree-climber, and its teeth mark it as one of the earliest metatherians, the line that leads to opossums, kangaroos and the other marsupials. It probably hunted insects among the branches.

A large, bell-shaped flagellate a few tenths of a millimetre long, covered at the front by thousands of flagella, that lives only in the hindgut of wood-eating termites such as dampwood termites. It engulfs the splinters of wood its host swallows and, with the help of its own bacteria, breaks down the cellulose that the termite could not digest alone. Host and protist depend on each other: termites cleared of their gut flagellates starve on a diet of wood.

A slimmer relative of the bell Trichonympha, named for the collar-like constriction behind its rostrum, living alongside other gut flagellates in the hindgut of dampwood termites. Like its relatives it swallows wood particles and digests their cellulose for its host. These protists are passed between termites when nestmates feed each other from the hindgut, and must be regained after every moult.

A blood-feeding leech of ponds, marshes and rice fields in East Asia, olive-green with yellowish-orange stripes along its back. It bites frogs and mammals, including people, with three toothed jaws inside its front sucker and keeps the blood flowing with anticoagulants in its saliva. It has long been used in traditional Chinese medicine.

A large, broad, flat leech of lakes, ponds and rice fields in China and neighbouring countries, growing to 10-12 cm. Despite its size it does not suck blood: its jaws are weak and it swallows snails, worms and insect larvae whole. It is farmed in China for traditional medicine.

A tiny marine leech, about a centimetre long, that lives its whole life on sea turtles, clinging to the soft skin of the neck, flippers and tail and feeding on their blood. Finger-like gills along the sides of its body take up oxygen from the water. It lays its cocoons on the turtle itself, so heavy infestations can build up on a single host.

A small land leech of damp mountain forests in Japan that waits on the forest floor and low plants for passing animals. It senses their warmth, breath and movement, loops toward them like an inchworm and sucks the blood of deer, wild boar and people. It has become more common in places where growing deer populations carry it around.

A small hard tick of eastern North American woodlands, also called the deer tick, and the main carrier of the bacteria that cause Lyme disease. Over a two-year life it takes three blood meals: larvae and nymphs mostly on mice, birds and lizards, adults on white-tailed deer. It waits for each host by 'questing' on low plants with its front legs held out.

A hard tick of the eastern and south-central United States, named for the single white spot on the female's back. It is an aggressive biter that will crawl towards a host, feeding on deer, wild turkeys and many other animals as well as people. It carries the bacteria that cause ehrlichiosis, and its bites are linked to alpha-gal syndrome, an allergy to red meat.

A small tick native to East Asia and long established in Australia and New Zealand, where it is a pest of cattle. Many populations are all female and reproduce parthenogenetically, each laying thousands of eggs without mating, so one tick can start a dense infestation. First found in the United States in 2017, it has since spread across much of the eastern states.

A third-of-a-millimetre mite that lives in house dust, bedding and upholstered furniture around the world, feeding on flakes of shed human and animal skin. It has no eyes and takes up water from humid air through its cuticle, so it thrives where the air is damp. Proteins in its droppings are one of the most common causes of indoor allergies and asthma.

A worm-shaped mite about 0.3 mm long that lives head-down in human hair follicles, mostly on the face, eyelashes and eyebrows. Its four pairs of stubby legs are crowded at the front of its body; it feeds on cells and oils inside the follicle and crawls out at night to mate. Most adults carry it without any symptoms.

A whitish mite under half a millimetre long that lives in the ear canals of cats, dogs, ferrets and foxes, feeding on skin debris and ear wax at the surface. Its front legs end in short stalked suckers. Heavy infestations cause intense itching and a dark, crumbly discharge, and it spreads easily between animals by contact.

A tiny blood-feeding mite of rats and other rodents, found worldwide wherever rats live, especially in warm climates. Rather than staying attached like a tick, it feeds briefly and then hides in the nest, and it can complete its life cycle in about two weeks. Greyish-white when hungry, it turns dark red after feeding. When its rodent hosts die or leave, it moves on to bite people, causing itchy dermatitis.

One of the world's most damaging plant pests, a half-millimetre mite recorded on more than a thousand kinds of plants. It pierces leaf cells and sucks out their contents, leaving pale speckles, and its colonies cover leaves in fine silk webbing. In warm weather a generation takes only about a week, so populations explode and quickly evolve resistance to pesticides.

A fast-running, bright orange-red mite that feeds almost only on spider mites, tracking them down by the smell of their webbing and damaged leaves. An adult can eat several spider mites or dozens of their eggs a day, and its numbers grow faster than its prey's. It is bred in huge numbers and released in greenhouses as one of the most widely used biological pest controls.

A chigger mite of South and Southeast Asia and northern Australia, and a main vector of scrub typhus. Only the tiny, six-legged orange-red larva is parasitic: it clings to a rodent, bird or person for a few days, feeding on skin tissue dissolved by its saliva, then drops off; nymphs and adults are free-living predators in the soil. The scrub typhus bacterium passes from mother mite to egg, so the mites themselves keep the infection going.

A ribbon-like flatworm usually two to three metres long that hangs in the human small intestine by a scolex armed with four suckers and a double crown of hooks, absorbing food through its skin. Its hundreds of proglottids ripen into egg-filled packets that are shed with the faeces; pigs that swallow the eggs carry the larvae as cysts in their muscles. People who swallow the eggs can develop cysticercosis, a leading cause of epilepsy in parts of the world.

The longest of the human tapeworms, commonly four to ten metres with a thousand or more proglottids, anchored by a small scolex with four suckers but no hooks. Its larvae develop as cysts in the muscles of cattle, and people are infected by eating undercooked beef. Ripe proglottids can crawl out of the host on their own, and an infection can last for decades.

A tiny tapeworm only three to six millimetres long, with a hooked scolex and usually just three proglottids, that lives by the thousands in the intestines of dogs and other canids. Sheep, cattle and other grazers that swallow its eggs grow fluid-filled hydatid cysts in the liver and lungs, inside which new scoleces bud off asexually. Dogs are infected by eating offal from these animals, and people who swallow the eggs can develop hydatid disease.

A tapeworm of the small intestine of cats and dogs that holds on with two slit-like grooves (bothria) instead of suckers, each of its proglottids carrying a coiled uterus. Its life cycle passes through tiny copepods in fresh water and then frogs, snakes and other vertebrates, where the larva, called a sparganum, wanders through the muscles as a white ribbon. People infected by eating raw frog or snake meat, or by poulticing wounds with frog flesh, develop sparganosis.

A small reddish-brown ant from the floodplains of central South America that has spread to the southern United States, Australia, China and elsewhere, mostly with shipped soil and plants. Colonies build loose earth mounds and swarm out to defend them, stinging repeatedly with a venom that leaves itchy pustules. During floods the workers link their bodies into living rafts that carry the queen and brood to dry land.

A small, plain brown ant from the Paraná River region of South America, now established in Mediterranean-climate regions on every inhabited continent. In its invaded range, nests that would normally fight one another treat each other as nestmates, forming supercolonies that can stretch for hundreds of kilometres. It feeds largely on the honeydew of sap-sucking insects and displaces many native ant species.

A tiny yellowish ant, about 2 millimetres long, probably native to tropical Asia but now found worldwide, mostly in heated buildings. Colonies have many queens and spread by budding, when a group of workers simply carries brood off to start a new nest. It is a persistent pest in homes and hospitals, where it can carry bacteria between rooms.

A tiny tropical ant, under 2 millimetres long, with a dark head and thorax but pale, almost translucent legs and abdomen, so it is hard to see on light surfaces. Spread around the world's tropics by trade, it nests in small crevices and moves its colonies often. Workers feed on honeydew, sweets and small insects.

A reddish-brown, spiny ant of the forests of Central and South America that cuts pieces of leaves and carries them back to its nest along cleared trails. The ants do not eat the leaves: they chew them into a mulch on which they grow a fungus that is the colony's main food and the only food of its larvae. A mature colony can hold millions of workers of very different sizes in a nest that reaches several metres underground.

A pale, comb-less flea about 2.5 millimetres long that lives mainly on rats, especially in warm climates, and bites people when its hosts die. It is the main carrier of the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis, which blocks its gut so that it regurgitates bacteria into each new bite, and it also spreads murine typhus. Like all fleas it is wingless, flattened from side to side and jumps with its long hind legs.

The commonest flea of both cats and dogs worldwide, a dark reddish-brown insect two to three millimetres long with a comb of spines under the head and another behind it, and a long, sloping forehead. Adults stay on the host and feed on blood, while the larvae live in bedding and carpets, eating debris and adult flea droppings. It can jump over a hundred times its own length and carries the cat-scratch bacterium and the dog tapeworm.

A close relative of the cat flea that lives on dogs, foxes and wolves and sometimes on cats and people, though in most places it is now rarer on dogs than the cat flea. It has the same two combs of spines but a shorter, more rounded head, and the first spine of the comb under the head is clearly shorter than the second. It too can carry the dog tapeworm.

A large sea snail of the rocky coasts of Japan, Korea and northern China that clamps onto rocks with its broad muscular foot and grazes on kelp and drifting seaweed. Water flows out through the row of open holes along its flattened, ear-shaped shell. Its meat and pearly shell have been prized for centuries, gathered by Japan's ama free divers, and its northern form, H. discus hannai, is one of the most widely farmed abalones.

South Africa's largest abalone, known locally as perlemoen, which lives on rocky shores and in kelp beds and feeds mostly on drift kelp and other seaweed. Its thick, ridged shell can reach about 20 cm, and young perlemoen shelter under the spines of sea urchins. Prized in East Asian markets, it is heavily poached by organised syndicates, and wild stocks have fallen so far that the legal fishery was closed for a time; most perlemoen sold today is farmed.

The largest living bivalve, which can grow over a metre long and weigh more than 200 kg, found on shallow reefs and lagoons of the western Pacific and eastern Indian Ocean. It lies hinge-down with its golden-brown mantle spread to the sun: besides filtering plankton, it farms photosynthetic algae (zooxanthellae) in its mantle that supply much of its food. Once settled it never moves again, and overharvesting for its meat and shell has wiped it out from many reefs, so it is listed as vulnerable.

The most widespread giant clam, found on reefs from the Red Sea and East Africa to Polynesia. It grows to about 20-30 cm and often sits partly sunk into the reef rock, its elongate, scaly shell hidden under a brilliant blue, green or patterned mantle that spreads over the shell's edges. Like other giant clams it filters plankton but gets much of its food from the photosynthetic zooxanthellae it farms in its mantle.

A rare giant clam of deep, dimly lit reef slopes around Tonga and Fiji, living deeper than most of its relatives. It has a relatively thin shell and a dull brownish mantle, yet still relies on photosynthetic zooxanthellae in its mantle as well as filtering plankton. It was described as a new species only in 1991, and some researchers now treat it as the same species as T. mbalavuana, first named from fossils.

The smallest giant clam, rarely more than 15 cm long, which bores into coral heads on shallow Indo-Pacific reefs until only its brilliant blue, purple or orange mantle shows at the surface. Sunk in the rock, it is safe from most predators while the zooxanthellae in its mantle soak up the sunlight and it filters plankton from the water. It can grow in dense patches on reef flats and is popular in the aquarium trade.

One of the oldest known bivalves, from the Early Cambrian of New York, Greenland and beyond: a tiny clam only about 4 mm long, its two smooth, thin, sideways-flattened valves joined by a straight hinge. It probably lay half buried in the sediment, digging with a muscular foot and drawing in water to feed. From little clams like it came the mussels, oysters, scallops and giant clams.

A small lingulid brachiopod about a centimetre long from the roughly 518-million-year-old Chengjiang biota of Yunnan, China. Its two thin, oval valves were made of calcium phosphate and protein rather than calcite. Because Chengjiang preserves soft tissue, its fossils still show the fringe of bristles around the shell margin and the long, fleshy stalk, or pedicle, that anchored it to the seabed, sometimes onto other shells. It strained food particles from the water with a ring of tentacles, the lophophore, inside the shell.

A spiriferid brachiopod from the Middle Devonian, about 385 million years ago, very common in the Hamilton Group shales of New York and Ontario. Its ribbed calcite shell is much wider than long, a few centimetres across, with the straight hinge line drawn out into long pointed wings, a raised fold down one valve and a matching groove in the other. It lay on the muddy sea floor, and inside the shell a pair of coiled calcite spirals supported its feeding tentacles.

A living lingulid brachiopod of Indo-Pacific tidal flats, with a thin, tongue-shaped greenish shell about 5 centimetres long. It lives upright in a vertical burrow in sand or mud, anchored by a long fleshy pedicle, with only the bristly front edge of the shell at the surface, where three funnels of bristles draw in and expel water. When disturbed it pulls itself down into the burrow. Often called a living fossil because its shell looks much like those of Cambrian lingulids, it tolerates low oxygen and changing salinity, and is eaten in parts of East Asia.

A fusulinid, one of the giant single-celled foraminifers of late Palaeozoic seas: a living cell inside a spindle-shaped, chambered calcite shell a few millimetres long, coiled around its long axis like a rice grain. It lived in warm, shallow late Carboniferous seas about 310 million years ago, in such numbers that its shells make up whole beds of limestone. It probably gathered food with thread-like pseudopods and, like large forams today, may have hosted algae in its cell.

A large fusulinid from the Early Permian, about 285 million years ago, described in 1937 from the Glass Mountains of West Texas. Its chambered calcite test, about a centimetre long, is a long, nearly cylindrical spindle with a straight middle and blunt ends, and its septa are folded into deep, regular flutes. This single-celled foraminifer lived on warm, shallow sea floors, probably with algae in its cell; today it is often placed in the genus Chalaroschwagerina.

A fusulinid named after the Hess Limestone of the Glass Mountains, West Texas, where its shells crowd Early Permian beds about 285 million years old. Its inflated, spindle-shaped test is under a centimetre long, with more pointed ends than its relatives and a thick, honeycomb-textured wall. Like other schwagerinids it is an index fossil: geologists use it to date and correlate Permian rocks across the American Southwest.

A stout fusulinid from Early Permian limestones of the Glass Mountains of West Texas, about 285 million years old, described in 1937. Its name means 'thick roof', for the heavy wall of its chambered calcite test, which is robust and swollen, under a centimetre long. A single cell lived inside, reaching out through the wall with thread-like pseudopods; vast numbers of such tests built up limestone on warm Permian shelves.

A slender, elongate fusulinid a few millimetres long from the Early Permian of the Glass Mountains of West Texas, about 285 million years ago, named in honour of the German geologist Carl Wilhelm von Gümbel. Its spindle-shaped test is narrower than those of its relatives, with finely fluted septa. Common in early Leonardian beds, it helps date Permian rocks; today it is often placed in the genus Praeskinnerella.

A large embolomere, a long-bodied relative of early tetrapods, from Late Carboniferous coal-swamp deposits of northern England about 310 million years old. It grew to perhaps four and a half metres, with a long, low skull lined with sharp teeth, small limbs and a long, deep, flattened tail. It probably lived much like a crocodile or a giant eel, swimming with side-to-side waves of its body and ambushing fish and smaller tetrapods in the swamp waters.

A roachoid, an early cockroach relative, from the Late Carboniferous coal measures of the English Midlands, preserved in ironstone nodules at Coseley near Dudley. Its holotype has been digitally reconstructed in three dimensions with X-ray micro-tomography, showing the broad shield-like pronotum over the head, the leathery forewings folded flat over the back and the spiny legs. Like other roachoids it probably foraged through the leaf litter of the coal swamp forests.

A large roachoid of the Late Carboniferous, known from fossil forewings found in Europe and North America. Its long forewings were densely veined, with many vein branches running out to the wing margin, and it was among the bigger cockroach relatives of the coal forests.

A roachoid of the family Spiloblattinidae from the latest Carboniferous of Commentry in central France, known from its forewings. Spiloblattinids had bold light-and-dark colour patterns on their forewings, and because these patterns changed from species to species through time they are used to date and correlate rocks of the Late Carboniferous and Early Permian.

A Late Carboniferous roachoid from France with long, narrow, densely veined forewings. Its name means 'sword-bearer': when Charles Brongniart described it in 1889 he noted the long external ovipositor of the female. Unlike modern cockroaches, which carry their eggs in a capsule, early roachoids like this one probably used their ovipositors to lay eggs one by one into soil or plant tissue.

One of the first beetle relatives, from the Early Permian insect beds of Tshekarda in the Urals, about 280 million years old. Its forewings had already hardened into elytra sculptured with rows of window-like cells, but they did not yet close over the back as in true beetles, leaving a narrow gap down the middle, and reached a little past the tip of the abdomen. Flat and long-legged, it probably lived under the bark of dead trees and in the leaf litter, the way of life that later made beetles the most varied animals on Earth.

An Eocene shark, about 56-34 million years ago, known only from its small teeth found in shallow-sea deposits of Europe and other regions. Its name links it to the whale shark, but it is now placed among the carpet sharks (Orectolobiformes), so its body is reconstructed here after living bottom-dwelling relatives such as nurse sharks, with nasal barbels and two dorsal fins set far back. It probably hunted small fish and invertebrates near the sea floor.

A narrow, elongated species of Dickinsonia from the Ediacara Hills of South Australia, with very many fine segments packed either side of its midline. Like its broader relatives it was a flat, soft-bodied animal that lay on the microbial mats of the shallow Ediacaran seafloor and probably fed on them through its underside.

A small, broad Dickinsonia from the White Sea coast of Russia, usually only a few centimetres long, with fewer and wider segments than its larger relatives. It is found on the same fossil-rich bedding surfaces as Yorgia and Kimberella, where it lived flat on the microbial mats that covered the seafloor.

A small shield-shaped animal, up to about 2.5 cm long, with a raised anchor-shaped ridge on its back. First found in the Ediacara Hills of South Australia and also known from the White Sea coast of Russia. Fossils are often aligned in the same direction, as if facing into a current.

A narrower species of Parvancorina described from Ediacaran rocks on the White Sea coast of Russia; its name means 'arrow'. Like its Australian relative it bore a raised anchor-shaped ridge on its back.

A small, slender Cloudina from the Nama Group of Namibia, its tubes only about a millimetre wide. Like its larger relative it built its tube as a stack of nested calcite funnels, making it one of the first animals with a mineralised skeleton. Some Cloudina tubes carry small bore holes, possibly among the earliest evidence of predation.

A Cloudina from the latest Ediacaran of Spain whose stacked funnel-shaped collars bear longitudinal ridges, giving the tube a fluted, spiny look. These ornamented tubes are among the oldest mineralised animal skeletons known.

A small calcified goblet on a slender stalk: a hollow cup with an opening on top and usually six round windows around its sides. First described from the Nama Group of Namibia, it grew alongside Cloudina in some of the earliest skeletal reefs. What kind of animal it was is still debated; some studies suggest a lophotrochozoan, a relative of brachiopods and bryozoans.

A frond from the Nama Group of Namibia and the namesake of the rangeomorphs. It is reconstructed with six vanes arranged around a central axis, each built of branches that repeat the same pattern at smaller and smaller scales. How it fed is uncertain; absorbing nutrients dissolved in seawater is one leading idea.

A broad, leaf-like frond from the very end of the Ediacaran, first found in the Nama Group of southern Namibia. It had three or more petal-like vanes quilted into tube-like units, held up on a long stalk. It was one of the last Ediacaran fronds, and how it fed is uncertain.

A flat disc with a central boss and many concentric rings, one of the most common Ediacaran fossils worldwide. It was first described from South Australia as a jellyfish, but it is now usually read as the buried holdfast of a frond or a microbial colony, so whether it fed by itself at all is unknown.

A tiny fossil, little more than a millimetre across, described in 2015 from the roughly 600-million-year-old Doushantuo Formation of Guizhou, China. It is made of three hollow tubes on a shared base, the largest opening into a wide funnel, and its cell-level preservation looks like a sponge's. If it was a sponge it filtered food from the water, but its identity is still debated.

An archaeocyath, one of the reef-building sponges of the early Cambrian, known from the archaeocyath limestones of South Australia. Its cylindrical-conical cup had two porous walls, with pores in neat vertical rows, joined by porous radial partitions, and it could grow alone or bud into small branching clumps. The genus was named in 1910 by Griffith Taylor, later a geologist on Scott's Antarctic expedition. Like other archaeocyaths it pumped seawater through its pores to filter out food.

A cup-shaped sponge from late Cambrian reef limestone of the Ellsworth Mountains, Antarctica, described in 1984 as an archaeocyath. For decades it was cited as the last surviving archaeocyath, far younger than all the others. A 2022 restudy of the original specimens found it was instead a lithistid demosponge, which suggests archaeocyaths had already died out by the middle Cambrian. It grew as slender double-walled cups, alone or budding into small clusters.

One of the oldest coral-like cnidarians with a hard skeleton, found in Cambrian rocks of western New South Wales, Australia, and North Greenland, about 510 million years old. Its colonies were clusters of cup-shaped corallites that budded from one another. Each cup had internal septa and was closed by a lid whose inner face also bore septa, something no living coral has. Its relationship to later corals is still debated.

A branching sponge up to about 8 cm tall from the roughly 505-million-year-old Burgess Shale of British Columbia, named after nearby Mount Vaux. Each branch is a slender, almost cylindrical tube with an open central cavity. Its skeleton was a net of flexible spongin fibres with no mineral spicules, like a modern bath sponge, making it one of the earliest known sponges of this kind. It was rare in Walcott's famous quarry but more common at other Burgess Shale sites.

A branching sponge described in 2021 from the roughly 518-million-year-old Chengjiang Biota of Yunnan, China, about 13 million years older than the Burgess Shale Vauxia. Its name means 'before gracilenta': it has the same two-layered net skeleton without spicules, but grew from a fan-like holdfast and had branches of very different sizes. Its discovery showed that sponges with organic skeletons had already diversified in the early Cambrian. Its full adult size is not well documented.

A long, thin, tube-shaped sponge from the early Cambrian Parker Slate of Vermont, about 514 million years old, and the type species of its genus. Specimens reach 7 to 12 cm long but are often only a few millimetres wide. Its wall was stiffened by long, parallel needle-like silica spicules running almost the full length of the body, over a layer of tiny crosswise spicules, and some fossils show a feathery spray of spicules at the top. Charles Walcott described it in 1886, and so far it is known only from that one Vermont locality.
