A small, common ichthyosaur about 1 metre long from the Middle Triassic of Monte San Giorgio on the Swiss-Italian border and elsewhere, about 242 million years ago. Fossils with traces of soft tissue show it had a tall dorsal fin, one of the earliest in an ichthyosaur, and its tail had a downward bend with a lower lobe. It is often seen as a halfway stage between eel-like early ichthyosaurs and the fast, tuna-shaped later ones, and it hunted fish and squid-like animals with its long, toothed snout.

A colossal early ichthyosaur about 17 metres long from the 246-million-year-old rocks of the Augusta Mountains in Nevada, described in 2021. Its skull alone was about 2 metres long, making it the first giant animal of the oceans, which reached whale size less than three million years after the first ichthyosaurs appeared. Unlike later ichthyosaurs it had a long, slender, eel-like body with no tall dorsal fin and only a gentle tail fin, and it hunted squid-like animals, fish and perhaps smaller marine reptiles.

A Middle Triassic ammonoid from the Muschelkalk sea of Germany, about 240 million years ago, with a shell about 10 cm across. Its flat-sided shell is crossed by strong ribs that swell into knobs at the edge of the broad, flat outer rim. It gave its name to the 'ceratitic' sutures, the lines where the chamber walls meet the shell, with smooth rounded saddles and finely toothed lobes. Ceratitid ammonoids flourished in the Triassic seas, and almost all died out at its end.

The commonest large predator of the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of the western United States, about 155-150 million years old. Adults reached about 8.5 metres, with a long, narrow skull bearing a short horn in front of each eye and a low ridge along each side of the snout. Rather than a crushing bite, it probably struck with its upper jaw like a hatchet, slicing with serrated teeth. Wounds on Stegosaurus and Allosaurus bones record fights between the two.

A Late Jurassic predator of the Morrison Formation, about 6 metres long, that shared its world with the larger Allosaurus. It had a blade-like horn on its nose, a low hornlet over each eye, extraordinarily long upper teeth and four fingers on short arms. Unusually for a theropod, a single row of small bony osteoderms ran down the middle of its back. Its deep, flexible tail has led some to suggest it hunted fish and other prey in wetlands.

One of the largest predators of the Early Jurassic, about 7 metres long, from the Kayenta Formation of Arizona, around 190 million years old. It is named for the pair of thin, half-moon crests along the top of its skull, probably used for display. A notch behind the narrow snout tip gave its upper jaw a kinked profile. The frill and venom of the Jurassic Park film are fiction; its real skull was strong and its teeth suited to large prey.

A small, lightly built theropod about one metre long, much of it tail, from the Late Jurassic lagoons of Bavaria and southern France, about 150 million years old. For over a century it was the smallest dinosaur known. Its long hind legs made it a fast runner, and the first skeleton has a whole lizard, Bavarisaurus, preserved in its stomach. Close relatives had a coat of simple filament feathers.

An early tyrannosauroid, a distant relative of Tyrannosaurus, about 3 metres long, from the Shishugou Formation of Xinjiang in China, about 160 million years old. Its name means 'crowned dragon', after the tall, thin, fan-like crest running along the middle of its snout. Unlike its giant descendants it had long, three-fingered arms. Two skeletons were found together in a pit, possibly mired in a bog formed by a sauropod footprint.

The best-known plated dinosaur, about 9 metres long, from the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of North America, about 155-150 million years old. Two staggered rows of broad bony plates ran down its arched back, probably for display, and four long spikes at the end of its tail made a formidable weapon. Its hind legs were far longer than its front legs, so it carried its tiny, narrow head close to the ground. It cropped low plants with a horny beak.

A stegosaur about 4.5 metres long from the Late Jurassic Tendaguru beds of Tanzania, about 152 million years old. Pairs of narrow plates on its neck and shoulders gave way to pairs of long, sharp spikes along its hips and tail, and a long spike jutted back from each shoulder. Studies of its tail suggest it could swing the spikes fast enough to inflict deep wounds. Over a thousand of its bones were found, though many were destroyed in Berlin during the Second World War.

One of the earliest armoured dinosaurs, about 4 metres long, from Early Jurassic rocks around 190 million years old near Charmouth in Dorset. It walked on all fours, with rows of oval, keeled bony scutes along its neck, back, flanks and tail, an early version of the armour of stegosaurs and ankylosaurs. Its skeleton, described by Richard Owen in the 1860s, was the first near-complete dinosaur ever found. It cropped plants with a small beak and leaf-shaped teeth.

One of the earliest and most primitive ornithischians, the beaked plant-eating dinosaurs that went on to include Stegosaurus, Triceratops and the duckbills. A small, swift biped about 1 m long from the Early Jurassic of Lesotho and South Africa, with long legs, short arms, big eyes, a horny beak at the tip of the snout and small leaf-shaped teeth for slicing plants. Some fossils were found curled up together, perhaps sheltering through a dry season.

A long, slender sauropod of the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation, about 154-152 million years old, reaching about 25 metres from snout to tail tip. Its very long neck was held out nearly level, letting it sweep across wide areas of ferns and horsetails, and its even longer tail tapered into a thin whiplash. Its small head had peg-like teeth only at the front of the jaws, used to strip leaves from branches. Casts of the skeleton nicknamed 'Dippy' stand in museums around the world.

A Late Jurassic sauropod from Sichuan in China, about 22 metres long, with one of the longest necks of any animal relative to its body. The neck made up nearly half its length and was built from 19 long, lightweight vertebrae braced by bony rods. It probably browsed over a wide arc of vegetation without moving its body. Its fossils come from river and lake deposits about 160 million years old.

A pigeon-sized scansoriopterygid dinosaur from rocks about 160 million years old in Hebei, China, described in 2015. Instead of feathered wings it had bat-like wings of skin stretched between its very long third finger and a long rod of bone at the wrist, a structure unknown in any other dinosaur. Its body was covered in filament-like feathers. It probably climbed trees and glided between them, an experiment in flight that left no descendants.

A crow-sized feathered dinosaur from western Liaoning, China, about 160 million years old, slightly older than Archaeopteryx. It had long flight feathers on its legs as well as its arms, giving it four wings. Melanosomes preserved in its feathers revealed its colours: a grey body, white wing feathers with black tips and a rufous crest. Pellets found with its skeletons contain lizard bones and fish scales, showing what it ate.

A long-tailed pterosaur from the Late Jurassic Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, about 150 million years old, with a wingspan of up to about 1.8 metres. Its long jaws held needle-like, forward-pointing teeth for catching fish, and its stiff tail ended in a diamond-shaped vane. Some fossils preserve fish in its throat, and one is locked in the jaws of the large fish Aspidorhynchus, which seized it as it skimmed the water.

An early pterosaur from the Early Jurassic cliffs of Lyme Regis in Dorset, about 195 million years old, first found by Mary Anning in 1828. It had a wingspan of about 1.4 metres and an enormous, deep skull lightened by large openings, carrying two kinds of teeth: long fangs at the front and small ones behind. Its short wings and strong claws suggest it was a poor long-distance flier that climbed well and snatched small animals on land.

The oldest known gliding mammal, a squirrel-sized animal from the Daohugou beds of Inner Mongolia, about 164-159 million years old. A furry skin membrane stretched between its front and hind limbs, preserved with hair impressions, and its long, flattened tail acted as a stabiliser. It belonged to the eutriconodonts, an extinct group of early mammals. Its sharp, pointed teeth suggest a diet of insects.

A semi-aquatic docodont, a close relative of true mammals, from Middle Jurassic lake deposits about 164 million years old in Inner Mongolia. About 45 cm long, it had dense fur, webbed, sprawling limbs for swimming and digging, and a broad, flat, scaly tail like a beaver's. Its recurved, seal-like teeth were suited to gripping fish and aquatic invertebrates. It showed that mammal relatives had taken to the water far earlier than once thought.

A long-necked plesiosaur about 4 metres long from the Middle Jurassic Oxford Clay of England, about 165 million years old. Its small, flat head carried many long, thin, interlocking teeth that formed a trap for small fish and squid-like cephalopods. It swam by 'flying' through the water with four long, pointed flippers. Many fine skeletons were dug from brick pits around Peterborough.

A fully marine relative of crocodiles, about 3 metres long, from the Middle to Late Jurassic seas of Europe, about 165-160 million years old. It had lost the bony armour of its land cousins and had paddle-like limbs and a shark-like tail fin with the larger lobe pointing down. Its long, narrow snout held conical teeth for catching fish and cephalopods. Salt glands in its head let it live at sea without fresh water.

A large marine crocodyliform, about 4-5 metres long, from Late Jurassic seas of Europe, about 157-145 million years old. Unlike its slender-snouted relatives it had a short, deep snout lined with large, serrated, blade-like teeth, earning a related species the nickname 'Godzilla'. It was a top predator able to cut up large prey such as marine reptiles. Like other metriorhynchids it had paddle limbs and a downturned tail fin.

A hybodont shark about 2 metres long from the Early Jurassic Posidonia Shale of Holzmaden, Germany, about 182 million years old. Hybodonts were a long-lived side branch of the sharks, with a stout, grooved bony spine in front of each of their two dorsal fins and a mix of pointed and crushing teeth. One famous skeleton has the remains of about 250 belemnites in its stomach. Males carried hooked spines on the head, probably used in mating.

A heavily armoured ray-finned fish of the Early Jurassic, a relative of today's gars, about one metre long. Its body was covered in thick, shiny, diamond-shaped ganoid scales set in diagonal rows. Rows of button-like teeth in its small mouth crushed snails and shellfish, and its fossils are common in the Toarcian rocks of Germany and England. Such teeth were once sold as 'toadstones', believed to protect against poison.

An ammonite of the Early Jurassic Toarcian seas, about 180 million years old, so widespread and short-lived that it marks a zone of time across Europe. Its flat, widely coiled shell, up to about 10 cm across, has a sharp keel flanked by two grooves, a smooth spiral groove along the middle of each side and sickle-shaped ribs on the outer half. It is named after St Hilda of Whitby, where its fossils are common. Legend said they were snakes turned to stone by the saint.

A sea lily of the Early Jurassic, about 195 million years old, that lived not on the seabed but hanging from floating driftwood in the open sea. Long, five-sided stems ringed with tendrils held crowns of densely branched, feathery arms that strained plankton from the water. At Lyme Regis in Dorset whole masses of them are preserved tangled around fossil logs. When the waterlogged wood finally sank, the colony died with it.

A horseshoe crab from the Late Jurassic Solnhofen lagoons of Bavaria, about 150 million years old, very like the living Limulus. It had a broad, domed head shield with compound eyes, a spiny hinged rear shield and a long, spike-like tail used to steer and flip itself over. Horseshoe crabs are chelicerates, closer to spiders and scorpions than to true crabs. One famous slab shows a Mesolimulus dead at the end of its own trackway, which it left as it wandered into the toxic lagoon floor.

A large prawn, around 15-20 cm long, from the Late Jurassic Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, about 150 million years old. Its first three pairs of legs were greatly elongated and fringed with long spines, forming a basket for snatching small swimming prey. It had a long, toothed rostrum and very long antennae. Fossils preserve it in such detail that the spines on its legs can be counted.

A giant lacewing from the Late Jurassic Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, about 150 million years old, with a wingspan of up to about 25 cm. Each of its four broad wings bore a large dark eyespot ringed with a pale band, much like the eyespots of butterflies, which appeared some 100 million years later. Kalligrammatids are called the 'butterflies of the Jurassic': relatives had long, tubular mouthparts for sipping sugary fluids from seed plants such as bennettitaleans.

A turkey-sized dromaeosaurid about 2 metres long, most of it tail, and some 15 kg, from the Late Cretaceous dunes of Mongolia about 75-71 million years ago. Quill knobs on its forearm show it had feathered wing-like arms, though it could not fly, and each foot carried an enlarged, raised sickle claw on the second toe. The famous 'Fighting Dinosaurs' fossil preserves one locked in combat with a Protoceratops, its claw in the plant-eater's throat.

A wolf-sized dromaeosaurid about 3.4 metres long from the Early Cretaceous of Montana and Wyoming, roughly 115-108 million years ago. Its name means 'terrible claw', after the big sickle claw on each foot. Its discovery in 1964 led John Ostrom to argue that dinosaurs were active, warm-blooded animals and closely related to birds, starting the 'Dinosaur Renaissance'. Its teeth are often found with skeletons of the plant-eater Tenontosaurus.

A bulky plant-eater about 10 metres long and several tonnes from the Early Cretaceous of Europe, around 126-122 million years ago, which could walk on four legs or rear up on two. Its hands combined hoof-like middle fingers, a grasping little finger and a conical thumb spike once mistaken for a nose horn. In 1878 coal miners at Bernissart in Belgium found dozens of skeletons together, more than 300 metres underground. It was only the second dinosaur ever named, in 1825.

A duck-billed dinosaur about 9.5 metres long from the Late Cretaceous of Alberta, about 76-74 million years ago. Its long, backward-curving head crest was a hollow tube of bone carrying the nasal passages; models of it produce a deep, trombone-like call, so it was probably used to communicate. Like other hadrosaurs it ground tough plants with batteries of hundreds of tightly packed teeth.

One of the largest duck-billed dinosaurs, around 9-12 metres long, from western North America about 73-68 million years ago. It had a long, low head with a broad toothless beak and no bony crest, but a mummified specimen shows a fleshy comb on top of its head. Huge bonebeds suggest it lived in large herds, and some skeletons carry healed Tyrannosaurus bite marks.

A two-legged plant-eater about 4.5 metres long from the very end of the Cretaceous in western North America, about 68-66 million years ago, alongside Tyrannosaurus and Triceratops. Its skull roof was a solid dome of bone up to 25 cm thick, ringed with bony knobs and spikes. Whether rivals rammed each other head-on or butted flanks is still debated, but healed injuries on many domes show they were used in combat.

A titanosaur from Patagonia about 96-92 million years ago and a candidate for the largest land animal ever, estimated at 30-35 metres long and some 65-75 tonnes. It is known from only a few huge bones, including vertebrae about 1.6 metres tall, so its size is reconstructed from relatives. Its eggs were probably only about the size of a football, and the hatchlings grew enormously fast.

An abelisaurid theropod about 7.5-8 metres long from the Late Cretaceous of Patagonia, about 72-69 million years ago. Its name means 'meat-eating bull', after the two thick horns above its eyes; its short, deep skull sat on a muscular neck and its arms were tiny stubs. It is one of the few dinosaurs known from extensive skin impressions, which show small scales with rows of larger conical bumps. Long legs and a powerful tail base suggest it was one of the fastest large theropods.

A carcharodontosaurid from Patagonia, about 99-97 million years ago, and one of the largest meat-eating dinosaurs, around 12-13 metres long and perhaps 6-8 tonnes, rivalling Tyrannosaurus. Its long, narrow skull carried thin, blade-like teeth suited to slicing flesh rather than crushing bone. It shared its world with giant titanosaurs such as Andesaurus.

A crow-sized dromaeosaurid about 80 cm long from the forests of north-eastern China around 120 million years ago. It had long flight feathers on its legs as well as its arms, giving it four wings, and a fan of feathers at the end of its tail, and probably glided and flapped between trees. Melanosomes show its plumage was glossy, iridescent black. Fossils preserve its last meals: a small mammal, a bird, a lizard and fish.

A small compsognathid about 1 metre long, more than half of it tail, from the Yixian Formation of north-eastern China, about 125 million years ago. Described in 1996, it was the first non-bird dinosaur found with a coat of feather-like filaments. Melanosomes show it was reddish-brown above and pale below, with a dark mask across its eyes and a tail ringed in ginger and white. One specimen has a lizard in its stomach.

A dog-sized early ceratopsian about 2 metres long from the Early Cretaceous of Mongolia and China, roughly 125-100 million years ago, and one of the best-known dinosaurs, with hundreds of specimens. It walked on two legs and cropped plants with a deep, parrot-like beak, and had a pointed horn on each cheek. A specimen with preserved skin shows long bristles along the top of its tail and countershaded colouring, darker above and lighter below, suited to a shady forest floor.

A sheep-sized horned-dinosaur relative about 1.8 metres long from the Gobi Desert of Mongolia, about 75-71 million years ago. It had a large head with a deep beak and a broad bony frill over the neck, but no true horns. Its fossils are so common that whole growth series from hatchlings to adults are known, and one is locked in a fight with a Velociraptor. It has been suggested, though it is disputed, that its beaked skulls inspired the legend of the griffin.

A giant, pot-bellied plant-eating theropod about 9-10 metres long from the Nemegt Formation of Mongolia, about 70 million years ago. Its hands carried three enormous claws, the bony cores alone over half a metre long, which it probably used to pull down branches and to defend itself rather than to kill. It had a small beaked head on a long neck and walked on short legs with four toes. Its first fossils, found in 1948, were thought to be from a giant turtle-like reptile, hence its species name.

An emu-sized oviraptorid about 2.9 metres long from the Gobi Desert of Mongolia, about 75 million years ago. It had a short, toothless beak and a tall rounded crest on its head. Several adults have been found sitting on nests of eggs with their feathered arms spread over them, showing that these dinosaurs brooded their eggs like birds. Its name refers to the skeleton-guardian lords of Tibetan Buddhist tradition.

A large, toothless pterosaur that soared over the inland sea of North America about 86-84 million years ago, with a wingspan of up to about 6-7 metres in the males. Males had a tall, backward-sweeping head crest; females were smaller with low crests. Fish remains found with its skeletons suggest it fed by plunging or skimming for fish far out at sea, like an albatross. Its name means 'wing without teeth'.

A large anhanguerid pterosaur from the Early Cretaceous of north-eastern Brazil, about 110 million years ago, with a wingspan of around 8 metres, the largest known from the southern hemisphere at that time. Tall, rounded keel-like crests on the tips of its upper and lower jaws may have steadied its head as it dipped into the water, and a rosette of long interlocking teeth at the front of its jaws snatched fish.

A long-necked plesiosaur about 10 metres long from the inland sea that covered Kansas about 80 million years ago. Its neck alone was some 7 metres long, with 72 vertebrae, more than any other known animal. It probably stalked schools of fish and squid, snaring them with long, interlocking teeth, and like other elasmosaurids it swallowed stones, perhaps as ballast or to grind food. When Edward Drinker Cope first described it in 1868 he put the head on the end of the tail.

The largest mosasaur, a giant marine lizard related to monitor lizards and snakes, about 11-13 metres long, from the seas of the last few million years of the Cretaceous, about 70-66 million years ago. It had massive jaws with thick conical teeth, four paddle limbs and a tail with a shark-like fluke. It was a top predator that ate fish, turtles, ammonites and other marine reptiles. A skull found near Maastricht in the Netherlands in the 1770s was one of the first fossils recognised as an extinct animal.

A huge mosasaur up to about 13 metres long from the inland sea of North America, about 86-80 million years ago. The front of its snout was a long, toothless, bony rostrum that it may have used to ram prey or rivals. Stomach contents show it ate almost anything: fish, sharks, diving birds such as Hesperornis, plesiosaurs and other mosasaurs.

A giant short-necked pliosaur about 9-10 metres long from the shallow inland sea that covered Queensland, Australia, about 110-100 million years ago. Its skull was over 2 metres long with big conical teeth up to 30 cm including the root. Stomach contents show it ate sea turtles and other plesiosaurs. A famous museum mount at Harvard made it look about 13 metres long because too many vertebrae were added.

The largest turtle known, about 4.6 metres long and over 2 tonnes, from the inland sea of North America about 80-74 million years ago. Its broad shell was a framework of bony ribs probably covered in tough leathery skin, like that of today's leatherback, and its front flippers spanned about 4 metres. It probably fed on soft-bodied prey such as jellyfish and squid and on shelled ammonites, which its hooked beak could crack.

A giant predatory bony fish about 5-6 metres long, shaped like an enormous tarpon, from the Late Cretaceous seas of North America and elsewhere. Its upturned, bulldog-like lower jaw bristled with long fangs. A famous fossil from Kansas, the 'fish-within-a-fish', has a 2-metre Gillicus swallowed whole inside it; the predator probably died from the struggling meal. It was in turn eaten by sharks and mosasaurs.

A large mackerel shark about 7-8 metres long that lived in seas worldwide from about 107 to 73 million years ago, built much like a stocky great white. Nicknamed the 'Ginsu shark' for its smooth, blade-like teeth, it was a top predator of the inland sea of North America. Bitten bones and teeth found in skeletons show it attacked mosasaurs, plesiosaurs and large fish.

A giant relative of alligators, perhaps 8-12 metres long, that lived in the coastal swamps and estuaries of southern North America about 82-75 million years ago. Its broad snout ended in a bulbous tip and was lined with huge blunt teeth, and its back was covered in deeply pitted osteoderms. Bite marks on turtle shells and on the bones of dinosaurs show it ambushed large prey at the water's edge.

Nicknamed 'SuperCroc', one of the largest crocodile-like reptiles, about 9-9.5 metres long and some 8 tonnes, from the rivers of what is now the Sahara in Niger, about 112 million years ago. It was not a true crocodile but a pholidosaur, an extinct side branch. Its long, fairly narrow snout ended in a bulbous expansion of unknown purpose, and it probably ate large fish and any dinosaur that came too close to the water.

A flightless diving bird up to about 1.8 metres long that hunted fish in the inland sea of North America about 86-80 million years ago. Its wings were reduced to tiny stubs, and it swam with powerful legs set far back on its body, ending in lobed toes like a grebe's. Its long beak still had small teeth set in a groove. On land it could probably only shuffle, so it likely came ashore just to breed.

A crow-sized early bird from the Jehol forests and lakes of north-eastern China, about 125-120 million years ago, and the oldest known bird with a toothless horny beak. Its wings still carried big clawed fingers, and many specimens, probably the males, have a pair of very long ribbon-like tail feathers. Thousands of fossils are known, sometimes many on one slab, and one preserves fish bones in its gut.

A badger-sized mammal about 1 metre long and 12-14 kg from the Yixian Formation of north-eastern China, about 125 million years ago, one of the largest mammals that lived alongside the dinosaurs. A specimen of its smaller relative Repenomamus robustus has the bones of a baby Psittacosaurus in its stomach, and another fossil shows one attacking an adult Psittacosaurus, so these mammals hunted small dinosaurs. It walked on short, sprawling legs and had strong jaws and teeth.

A straight-shelled heteromorph ammonite from the inland sea of North America, about 73 million years ago. After a tiny initial coil only millimetres across, its shell grew as a long, slightly flattened rod, often more than half a metre long, with crescent-shaped ribs and frilly sutures between the gas-filled chambers. Jaws found inside the shells suggest it fed on plankton. Its fossils are so abundant in the Pierre Shale that successive Baculites species are used to date the rocks.

A tiny insect about 3 mm long, preserved in Burmese amber about 99 million years old and described in 2006 as the oldest known bee-like fossil. It combined wasp-like features, such as slender hind legs, with the branched body hairs that bees use to collect pollen, so it probably fed at the early flowers that were then spreading. Pollinating insects like it helped flowering plants spread and diversify across the world during the Cretaceous.

A fox-sized early horse of the early Eocene forests of North America, about 60 cm long and 30 cm high at the shoulder. It had four hoofed toes on the front feet and three on the hind, an arched back and low-crowned teeth for browsing soft leaves and fruit. Long known as Hyracotherium, the American dawn horses are now usually placed in Eohippus and its relatives.

A three-toed horse of the late Eocene and Oligocene of North America, about 60 cm at the shoulder. Longer legs, a longer face and a larger brain than the dawn horses suited the drier, more open woodlands of its time, where it browsed leaves and shrubs. Its middle toe already carried most of its weight.

A rhino-sized browser of the middle Eocene of North America, about 4 m long and 1.5 m at the shoulder. Its long, flat skull bore three pairs of blunt bony knobs, and males had long, dagger-like upper canines guarded by a flange on the lower jaw, probably used for display and fighting. Its brain was remarkably small for its size.

A sheep-sized early hoofed mammal of the late Paleocene and early Eocene of North America and Europe, about 1.5 m long. Phenacodus had a long low body, a long heavy tail and five toes on each foot ending in small hooves, the middle one the largest: the plan from which horses, rhinos and the other hoofed mammals grew. It browsed and ate fruit in open woodland.

A hippo-like pantodont about 2.25 m long that lived around the swamps and rivers of Europe and North America in the latest Paleocene and early Eocene, reaching even the warm forests of the Arctic. It had stout, short legs, a heavy body and tusk-like canines, and it browsed soft water plants and leaves. It was one of the largest mammals of its time.

A heavy pantodont of the late Paleocene of North America, about 2.5 m long and weighing some 600 kg, one of the first large mammals after the dinosaurs. It had a small head, massive hindquarters and a very thick tail that may have propped it up while it reared to browse leaves.

A giant mammal of the middle Eocene of Inner Mongolia known only from an 83 cm skull, the largest of any meat-eating land mammal. Long thought to be a mesonychid, it is now usually considered a relative of the entelodonts and hippos, so it probably had hoofed toes. Its big blunt teeth suggest it ate almost anything, from carrion and bones to shellfish and tough plants.

A hornless rhinoceros of the Oligocene of Central Asia and one of the largest land mammals that ever lived, about 4.8 m at the shoulder, 7-8 m long and 15-20 tonnes. Long pillar-like legs and a long neck let it browse leaves high in trees like a giraffe, pulling them in with a mobile upper lip and tusk-like incisors. It was also known as Indricotherium and Baluchitherium.

A rhino-like mammal of the late Eocene and early Oligocene of North and East Africa, about 3 m long, best known from the Fayum of Egypt. It belonged to the embrithopods, distant relatives of elephants and hyraxes, and carried two huge, hollow conical horns side by side above its nose. It browsed tough leaves in coastal swamp forests.

An early relative of elephants from the late Eocene of North Africa that looked more like a pygmy hippo or tapir, about 70 cm at the shoulder. It had no trunk, only a mobile upper lip, and short tusk-like incisors in both jaws. Chemistry of its teeth shows it lived in rivers and swamps and fed on water plants.

A wolf-sized hyaenodont of the late Eocene and Oligocene of North America. Hyaenodonts were an ancient group of meat-eating mammals unrelated to dogs or cats, with a long, narrow skull and three pairs of blade-like shearing teeth. It hunted early horses, camels and entelodonts and scavenged carcasses.

An entelodont, one of the pig-like "hell pigs" of the late Eocene and Oligocene of North America, about 1.2 m at the shoulder. Its huge head carried bony flanges under the eyes and knobs under the chin, and bite marks show rivals fought by gripping each other's faces. It dug for roots and tubers, scavenged, and cached the carcasses of small camels it had killed.

A brontothere ("thunder beast") of the late Eocene of North America, about 2.5 m at the shoulder, a distant relative of horses and rhinos. It had a hump over its shoulders and a blunt, forked bony horn on its nose, larger in males and probably used in shoving contests. It browsed soft leaves, and the brontotheres died out as the climate cooled at the end of the Eocene.

A raccoon-sized even-toed ungulate of the middle Eocene of Kashmir, about 40 cm long, like a small mousedeer on long slender legs. It is the closest known relative of the whales: its ear bones already had the thick, shell-like wall of a whale's, and its heavy limb bones weighed it down in water, where it probably waded and hid from predators, as the African water chevrotain does today.

One of the earliest whales, from the early Eocene of Pakistan about 50 million years ago. It was a wolf-sized land mammal with slender legs, small hooves and a long tail that waded in shallow streams, but its ear bones already had the thick, shell-like form of a whale's. Its eyes sat on top of its long head, like a crocodile's.

The "walking swimming whale" of the early Eocene of Pakistan, about 3 m long. It lived like a crocodile in estuaries and coastal rivers, with short legs, huge paddle-like hind feet and a long, powerful tail. It probably lurked in the shallows to ambush animals that came to drink, and could drink both fresh and salt water.

A protocetid whale of the middle Eocene of Pakistan, about 3 m long, that still had four working legs. It swam by paddling with its big webbed hind feet and undulating its long tail, which had no fluke, and could probably still haul out onto the shore like a sea lion. It hunted fish in the warm shallow Tethys Sea.

A huge, eel-like whale of the late Eocene, 15-18 m long, found around the Gulf of Mexico and the Tethys Sea. Its very long body was built of elongated vertebrae, its flippers were small, and it kept tiny hind legs that were no use for walking. It was the top predator of its seas, and stomach contents and bite marks show it ate fish and the young of the smaller whale Dorudon.

A dolphin-shaped whale of the late Eocene, about 5 m long, best known from the fossil whale valley of Wadi Al-Hitan in Egypt. It swam with a tail fluke like modern whales but still had tiny hind legs, and it ate fish with large shearing teeth. Many juvenile skulls bear the bite marks of Basilosaurus.

The largest snake ever found, a relative of boas and anacondas from the middle to late Paleocene of Colombia, about 13 m long and weighing over a tonne. It lived in the hot rainforest rivers of the Cerrejon Formation a few million years after the dinosaurs died out, and probably hunted fish and crocodile relatives. Its size suggests the tropics were then several degrees warmer than today.

A giant constricting snake from the late Eocene of Egypt's Fayum, estimated at 7-10 m long and long thought the largest snake until Titanoboa was found. It belonged to the madtsoiids, an ancient family of snakes unrelated to boas and pythons that survived in Australia until the Pleistocene. It probably ambushed large prey such as early relatives of elephants.

One of the earliest known snakes, about 2 m long, from the roughly 95-million-year-old Candeleros Formation of Rio Negro, Argentina. It is a true transitional form: its skull still had a cheek bone that later snakes lost, and it kept a small pair of hind legs with a pelvis joined to the spine, beside the vent. It lived on land in a dry, desert-like setting and probably hunted from burrows, which suggests that snakes lost their legs on land rather than in the sea.

A giant flightless bird of the late Paleocene and early Eocene of North America (once called Diatryma), about 2 m tall and up to 175 kg. Its huge, deep beak was long pictured killing early horses, but its bite mechanics, the lack of a hooked tip and the chemistry of its bones suggest it cracked nuts, seeds and tough plants. It was a relative of ducks and geese.

An early relative of ducks from the late Paleocene and early Eocene of North America that looked like a duck on a flamingo's legs. It nested in huge colonies on the shores of shallow, salty lakes such as the Green River lakes of Wyoming, where thousands of its bones and eggshells are found. It strained plankton and small plants from the water with its broad, flat bill.

One of the oldest members of the modern bird groups, a relative of ducks and geese from the last few million years of the Cretaceous on Vega Island, Antarctica, when the continent was still forested. It was a foot-propelled diver about 60 cm long with a loon-like body and large webbed feet, and it preserves the oldest known syrinx, the voice box of birds, which suggests it honked. It shows that the lines of modern birds had already split before the dinosaurs died out.

One of the oldest and largest penguins, from the late Paleocene of New Zealand, about 1.6 m long and perhaps 100 kg. It shows that penguins became flightless, wing-propelled divers and giants within a few million years of the end-Cretaceous extinction. It had a long, narrow beak for catching fish and squid.

One of the oldest well-preserved bats, from the early Eocene lake beds of Wyoming's Green River Formation, about 14 cm long with a 37 cm wingspan. It already flew and probably echolocated like living insect-eating bats, but kept a claw on its index finger and a long tail. Moth scales have been found in its stomach.

A small bat from the middle Eocene Messel pit in Germany, with a wingspan of about 30 cm and among the commonest fossils there. Its short, broad wings suited slow, agile flight low over the lake and under the trees, and its stomach contents show it ate moths and caddisflies. Pigment cells preserved in its fur indicate it was reddish-brown.

A small herring of the early Eocene Green River lakes of Wyoming, usually 10-15 cm long and one of the most common fossil fish in the world; whole schools are preserved together in the lake beds. It fed on plankton and small insects and was eaten by gars, larger fish, birds and turtles.

One of the earliest teleosts, the group that now makes up almost all living fish, from the Early Jurassic seas of Europe. About 15 cm long and herring-like, it had thin, round scales instead of the heavy enamelled scales of older fish, a symmetrical forked tail and a single dorsal fin. It swam in great shoals and was eaten by ichthyosaurs, pterosaurs and larger fish.

A small insectivore from the middle Eocene of Europe, best known from complete skeletons from the Messel pit, 60-90 cm long including a tail longer than its body. Its long hind legs and short arms suggest it ran or hopped on two legs over the forest floor, and it probed for insects, lizards and small mammals with a long, mobile snout. It belonged to the leptictids, an extinct side branch of early placental mammals.

A rat-sized mammal from rocks in Montana laid down within a few hundred thousand years of the asteroid impact that ended the age of dinosaurs, and one of the earliest undoubted placental mammals. Its low, blunt-cusped teeth could crush fruit and seeds as well as insects, and it was long thought to stand near the ancestry of the hoofed mammals. In the emptied world after the extinction, animals like it gave rise to the great radiation of placentals.

A lemur-like primate from the middle Eocene Messel pit in Germany, known from "Ida", an almost complete skeleton with fur outline and a last meal of fruit and leaves. It was about 58 cm long, more than half of it tail, with grasping hands and feet bearing nails. It belongs to the adapiforms, an extinct branch related to lemurs and lorises.

An early catarrhine primate from the early Oligocene of the Fayum in Egypt, close to the common ancestor of Old World monkeys and apes. About the size of a howler monkey, it climbed slowly through swampy tropical forest eating fruit. It had a longer snout and smaller brain than later monkeys, and males were larger than females.

A squirrel-like relative of the primates from the late Paleocene of Europe, about 60 cm long with a long bushy tail. It had claws instead of nails, eyes on the sides of its head and big gnawing front teeth like a rodent's. It climbed trees and fed on leaves, seeds and fruit.

The earliest known plesiadapiform, the stem group of the primates, from the very beginning of the Paleocene of Montana, about 66 million years ago. Squirrel-sized, with a long tail, it is known from teeth, jaws and ankle bones; the ankles show it could turn its feet to grip and climb down tree trunks. Its teeth suited a diet of fruit and insects in the new flowering forests.

A leopard-sized "false sabre-tooth" of the early Oligocene of North America. Nimravids were cat-like carnivores that evolved long, flattened upper canines independently of the true sabre-toothed cats, sheathed by a bony flange on the lower jaw. It had a long, low body, short powerful legs and probably ambushed early horses and other mammals.

A small, tree-climbing meat-eater of the Eocene forests of North America, about 30 cm long plus a long bushy tail, built like a genet. Miacids sit near the root of the carnivorans: they already had the pair of blade-like shearing teeth of the cats, dogs and bears that came after them, and flexible ankles for climbing down trunks head first.

The largest entelodont or "hell pig", about 1.8 m tall at the shoulder, from the latest Oligocene and Early Miocene of North America. Its huge head had bony flanges under the cheeks and knobs under the chin, and its teeth could crack bones. Entelodonts were not true pigs but relatives of whales and hippos; Daeodon probably scavenged carcasses and ate roots and fruit.

One of the largest land mammals ever, standing about 4 m at the shoulder, from the Middle and Late Miocene of Europe. Unlike elephants it had no upper tusks; instead a pair of thick lower tusks curved down and back from the tip of its lower jaw, probably used to strip bark and pull down branches. Its long legs suggest it walked long distances through open woodland. Deinotheres were a side branch of the proboscideans that died out in the Early Pleistocene.

The "shovel-tusker", an elephant relative of the Middle Miocene of China, Mongolia and Kazakhstan, about 3 m tall. Its very long lower jaw ended in two broad, flat incisors forming a scoop, and a broad trunk rested on top of it. Once thought to shovel water plants, it is now thought to have cut and stripped branches and bark with the sharp edge of its scoop.

A widespread elephant relative of the Middle Miocene of Europe, about 3 m at the shoulder. It had four tusks: two long upper tusks curving down and forward, and two shorter, straight lower tusks on a long lower jaw. Gomphotheres spread from Africa across Eurasia when the two continents joined about 19 million years ago and later reached the Americas.

A strange relative of horses and rhinos from the Middle Miocene of Europe, about 2.6 m tall at the shoulder. Its long forelimbs and short hind legs gave it a gorilla-like sloping back, and it walked on its knuckles to keep its long hooked claws sharp. It probably sat or stood up on its hind legs to pull down branches with its claws.

A pony-sized, three-toed horse of the Late Miocene of Greece and Turkey, known from rich fossil beds such as Pikermi and Samos. Hipparionine horses crossed from North America into the Old World about 11 million years ago and spread so fast that their arrival is used to date rocks. It ran on its central toe, the two small side toes held off the ground.

An early grazing horse of the Middle Miocene North American plains, about 1 m tall at the shoulder. It was one of the first horses with high-crowned teeth able to grind tough, gritty grass as grasslands spread. It still had three toes on each foot, but stood on the central hoof, with long legs for running.

A hippo-like rhinoceros of the Miocene of North America, with a long barrel-shaped body, very short legs and a small horn on the tip of its nose. Herds of over a hundred were buried by volcanic ash about 12 million years ago at Ashfall Fossil Beds in Nebraska, some with their last meal of grass in their throats and calves beside their mothers.

The "giraffe camel" of the Middle and Late Miocene of North America, where camels first evolved. A humpless camel with very long, slender legs and a long neck, it held its small head about 3 m above the ground to browse on trees like a giraffe. Like modern camels it walked on padded feet with two toes.

One of the largest "bear-dogs", from the Middle Miocene of North America, weighing perhaps 500 kg. Amphicyonids were carnivorans with a bear-like body, a wolf-like head and a long, heavy tail. Its strong forelimbs suggest it grappled with large prey such as horses and camels.

A chimpanzee-sized great ape of the Middle and Late Miocene of the Siwalik Hills of India and Pakistan, about 12.5 to 8.5 million years ago. Its concave face and narrow space between the eyes are very like an orangutan's, and it is thought to be close to that lineage. It lived in forests and ate fruit, moving both in trees and on the ground.

An early hominin of East Africa from about 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago, best known from the skeleton "Lucy" found in Ethiopia in 1974. It walked fully upright, as the 3.7-million-year-old Laetoli footprints show, but kept long arms and curved fingers for climbing. It stood 1.1 to 1.5 m tall and had a brain about a third the size of ours.

An early hominin that lived in woodland in Ethiopia about 4.4 million years ago, known from the partial skeleton "Ardi". It walked upright on the ground but kept an opposable big toe for grasping branches, a mix never seen in a living ape. Males had small canines, which may mean less fighting between them than in chimpanzees.

A massive okapi-like giraffid of the Pliocene and Early Pleistocene of the Indian subcontinent, weighing over a tonne, among the heaviest ruminants ever. It had a short, thick neck and two pairs of ossicones: large, branching, palm-like ones at the back of the skull and small cones above the eyes. Related forms lived in Africa well into the Pleistocene.

A giraffid of the Late Miocene of Samos in Greece and Turkey, with a neck about half way in length between the okapi's and the giraffe's, and two long ossicones sweeping back above its eyes. Its neck bones show how the giraffe's long neck evolved in steps. Worn teeth suggest it grazed as well as browsed.

A jaguar-sized predator of the Late Miocene and Pliocene of Argentina, a sparassodont related to marsupials that evolved a sabre-toothed body like the cats on its own. Its huge upper canines grew throughout life, their roots reaching back over the eyes, and were sheathed by deep bony flanges on the lower jaw. Unlike sabre-toothed cats it had no lower incisors, and some think it ate soft insides of carcasses.

A flightless "terror bird" about 2.5 m tall from the Early and Middle Miocene of Patagonia, which gave the family Phorusrhacidae its name. It had long running legs, tiny wings and a huge head with a deep, hooked beak. It probably struck prey with rapid downward blows of the beak, like the seriema, its closest living relative.

A terror bird of the Middle Miocene of Patagonia, about 15 million years ago, with the largest bird skull known: 71 cm long, most of it a narrow, hooked beak. Its long, slender lower legs suggest it was a fast runner despite standing about 3 m tall. It is known from a single skull and leg bone found in 2006.

One of the largest flying birds known, from the Late Miocene of Argentina, with a wingspan of about 6-7 m and a weight of some 70 kg. A teratorn, related to New World vultures, it was too heavy to flap for long and must have soared on the strong westerly winds and thermals off the Andes. Its large, hooked bill suggests it swallowed small prey whole as well as scavenging.

A giant seabird of the Late Miocene of Chile with a wingspan of about 5.2 m, known from an unusually complete skeleton. Its long bill was lined with sharp, tooth-like spikes of bone (pseudo-teeth) for gripping fish and squid. Like albatrosses it glided over the open ocean on long, narrow wings; pelagornithids flew the world's seas for about 50 million years before vanishing in the Pliocene.

A raptorial sperm whale of the Late Miocene of Peru, about 9 million years ago, perhaps 13-17 m long. Its teeth, up to 36 cm long in both jaws, are the largest of any animal used for eating, and it probably hunted baleen whales, competing with Megalodon. It was named after the biblical Leviathan and Herman Melville, author of Moby-Dick.

A small whale related to narwhals from the Late Miocene and Pliocene of Peru that evolved a walrus-like face. It had a blunt, beakless snout with a muscular upper lip for sucking clams from the sea floor, eyes facing forward and up, and two tusks pointing backwards along the body; in males the right tusk was much longer, over a metre.

A ground sloth of the Late Miocene coast of Peru that waded and swam into the sea to graze on seagrass and seaweed, because the land behind the coast was desert. Over several million years its species became more aquatic, with denser bones for ballast, a longer snout and a broad, spatula-shaped mouth for cropping. It probably held on to the sea floor with its long curved claws.

A giant caiman of the Late Miocene wetlands of the western Amazon, about 8 million years ago, probably 10-12 m long and weighing several tonnes, among the largest crocodylians ever. Its broad skull was about 1.4 m long and its bite was one of the strongest known. It could have taken almost any animal in its swamps, including giant turtles and large mammals.

A giant side-necked turtle of the Middle and Late Miocene rivers and lakes of northern South America, with a shell up to about 2.4-2.9 m long, one of the largest turtles ever. Males had two stout horns on the front of the shell, probably used in fights. Fossils show bite marks from crocodylians, and it ate plants, seeds, fish and molluscs.

A giant relative of piranhas and pacus from the Late Miocene of Argentina, about 8-10 million years ago. Known only from part of a jaw, it had a zig-zag row of teeth halfway between the double row of pacus and the single row of piranhas. It was probably 70 cm to 1 m long and may have had one of the strongest bites for its size of any fish.

A hippo-like marine mammal of the Middle Miocene coasts of the North Pacific, from Japan to California. Desmostylians are the only order of marine mammals that has completely died out; its name means "bundle of pillars", from the shape of its molar teeth. It had forward-pointing tusks in both jaws and probably grazed seagrass and algae in shallow water.

A lion-sized bone-cracking carnivore of the Late Miocene of Eurasia and Africa, a percrocutid, related to hyenas and cats rather than a true hyena. It had a massive head with a short muzzle and powerful jaws able to crush bones. Fossil bones chewed by it suggest it both hunted and scavenged large herbivores.

A burrowing rodent about 30 cm long from the Late Miocene and Early Pliocene of the North American Great Plains, the smallest mammal known to have had horns. A pair of bony horns rose from its nose, perhaps for defence or display rather than digging. It dug with big claws on its front feet and had tiny eyes, like modern pocket gophers.

A giant gymnure, a hairy relative of hedgehogs, from the Late Miocene island of Gargano in Italy. It grew to about the size of a cat, with a long, cone-shaped snout, coarse fur instead of spines and a long naked tail. Like many island animals it grew large in the absence of competitors, and it probably ate insects, snails, small vertebrates and carrion.

A giant rhinoceros of the Pleistocene steppes from the Black Sea to Kazakhstan and Mongolia, about 2 m tall and weighing up to 4 tonnes. A huge bony dome on its forehead is thought to have carried a single long horn. It grazed tough grasses and survived until about 39,000 years ago.

A rhinoceros of the Ice Age mammoth steppe of northern Eurasia, covered in long, thick hair and with small ears and a short tail to save heat. Its front horn could be over a metre long and was flattened from side to side, worn on the front by sweeping snow off grass. Stone Age people painted it in Chauvet Cave, and it died out about 14,000 years ago.

A giant deer of Pleistocene Eurasia, standing about 2 m at the shoulder, whose males grew the largest antlers of any deer, up to 3.6 m across and 40 kg, shed and regrown each year. It was not an elk but a relative of the fallow deer, and is called Irish because so many skeletons were dug from Irish bogs. It survived in western Siberia until about 7,700 years ago.

The largest marsupial that ever lived, a wombat relative the size of a hippopotamus, weighing up to 2.7 tonnes. It roamed the open woodlands and grasslands of Pleistocene Australia, and fossils suggest it migrated with the seasons. Like other marsupials it carried its young in a pouch; it died out about 40,000 years ago, after people reached Australia.

A leopard-sized marsupial predator of Pleistocene Australia, related to wombats and koalas. Pound for pound it had one of the strongest bites of any mammal, with blade-like cheek teeth instead of long canines, and a huge claw on each thumb. Scratch marks in caves show it could climb, and it may have dropped on prey from trees.

A car-sized armadillo relative of Pleistocene South America, weighing up to 2 tonnes. Its domed shell, about 1.5 m tall, was made of over a thousand fused bony plates, and it had a bony cap on its head and a tail armoured with rings of plates. It grazed near rivers and lakes and died out about 10,000 years ago; early people may have used its shells as shelters.

The tallest bird ever known, from New Zealand's South Island: females could reach 3.6 m with the neck raised and weighed up to 250 kg, far more than the males. Moa had no wings at all and browsed on twigs and leaves in forest and scrub, with only the giant Haast's eagle to fear. All moa were hunted to extinction within about 200 years of people arriving, around 1400 AD.

One of the largest carnivorous land mammals, a bear of Pleistocene North America that stood about 1.6 m at the shoulder on all fours and weighed up to 900 kg. Its long legs and short face once suggested a fast hunter, but studies of its bones point to a varied diet, with much scavenging of large carcasses. It died out about 11,000 years ago.

A camel-like hoofed mammal of Pleistocene South America with a long neck, three-toed feet and nostrils high on its head, often shown with a short trunk. Charles Darwin found its bones in 1834 and thought it was a giant llama. Ancient proteins show its group, the litopterns, were related to horses and rhinos; it died out about 10,000 years ago.

A rhinoceros-sized hoofed mammal of Pleistocene South America, with a barrel body, short legs and a broad head with ever-growing teeth. Darwin collected its skull in Uruguay during the voyage of the Beagle. It belonged to the notoungulates, a native South American group distantly related to horses and rhinos.

Our closest extinct relatives, who lived in Europe and western Asia from about 400,000 to 40,000 years ago. They were stocky and strong, with a large brain, a long low skull and a heavy brow, and were skilled hunters of large animals who made stone tools, controlled fire and buried their dead. Most people living today outside Africa carry a little Neanderthal DNA.

A huge, soft-bodied relative of the arthropods up to about half a metre long from Sirius Passet in northern Greenland, about 518 million years old. It had a pair of big spiny grasping limbs at the front, a mouth ringed with hard plates, eleven pairs of swimming flaps along its sides and stubby legs beneath. Large and powerful, it was one of the top predators of its sea, though its unarmoured body is easy to wound.

A small radiodont about 6 cm long from the Chengjiang biota of Yunnan, China, about 518 million years old, its name meaning "lyre-tailed predator with claw-like spines". Its frontal limbs carried long, curved spines that worked like grasping claws, and some fossils even preserve its brain. Quick, sharp-eyed and armed with those claws, it struck hard for its size, but its small body could not take much punishment.

A 10 cm arthropod from the Burgess Shale of Canada with a broad two-halved shell over its head, a long body of about fifty segments with many small legs, and a pair of big pincer-like claws at the front. Its name means "grasping", and those claws, together with simple jaws, helped it seize and break up soft prey. It is one of the earliest known relatives of crabs, insects and centipedes, and a hard-hitting hunter of the seafloor.

A giant arrow worm about 10 cm long from the Burgess Shale of Canada, far larger than the living arrow worms. Its head bore a crown of about 50 curved grasping spines that snapped shut over prey, and its slim body ended in fins for darting through the water. A deadly ambusher with a terrible bite, it has almost no protection when attacked.

One of the largest animals of its time, a radiodont about half a metre long from the Burgess Shale of Canada, whose head was covered by an enormous flattened shell. It swam low over the seabed, raking the mud with comb-like front limbs for small animals. Its sheer bulk and huge armoured head make it extremely hard to bring down, but it is a slow, clumsy swimmer and not a strong fighter.

A spiny, soft-legged animal about 8.5 cm long from the Xiaoshiba biota of Yunnan, China, nicknamed "the hairy Collins' monster". Its back carried 72 sharp spines, up to five per body segment, while six pairs of feathery front legs combed food from the water and nine pairs of clawed hind legs held it in place. Bristling with spines, it is almost impossible to attack safely, but it is slow and weak in a fight.

A slug-like animal up to about 8 cm long from Sirius Passet in northern Greenland, covered in a coat of mail made of some two thousand small overlapping scales, with a rounded shell at each end of its back. It crawled over the seabed grazing microbial films, and it is thought to be an early relative of molluscs or brachiopods. Wrapped in armour from head to tail, it shrugs off most attacks, but it is slow and has no weapons.

A vase-shaped animal around 10 cm tall from the Burgess Shale of Canada, fixed to the seabed and covered in star-shaped clusters of sharp, radiating spines. It probably fed like a sponge, drawing water in through its soft body and out through an opening at the top. Its forest of spines makes it a painful mouthful, and it can take a lot of damage before giving way, though it cannot move or strike.

A flat, kite-shaped swimmer about 5 cm long from the Burgess Shale of Canada, with a fin running along each side, a pair of stalked eyes and two long, flexible tentacles at the front. Some think it was an early relative of squid and octopuses that pushed water out through a funnel under its body to jet along. One of the fastest swimmers of its time, it hunts on the move and escapes easily, but its soft body breaks at the first blow.

A tiny eel-like fish about 3 cm long from the Chengjiang biota of Yunnan, China, about 518 million years old, and one of the earliest known vertebrates. It had a long, slender body, a pair of eyes and a short snout at the front, and no jaws. Built for darting through the water, it is very hard to catch, though it has no armour or weapons at all.

A small swimming arthropod about 3 cm long from the Chengjiang biota of Yunnan, China, enclosed in a thin two-halved shell drawn out into long spines at the front and back. It had big round eyes and a pair of spiny grasping limbs to catch small animals as it swam in open water. Fast and keen-sighted, it moves and hunts well, but its light shell gives only modest protection.

A worm-like relative of velvet worms about 7 cm long from the Chengjiang biota of Yunnan, China, with five pairs of spiny arms at the front and no legs behind. Its swollen rear end was lodged in a tube in the seabed, while its arms swept food from the water. When danger came it could pull back into its tube, so it is very hard to catch, but it can barely move.

A tulip-shaped animal up to 20 cm tall from the Burgess Shale of Canada: a cup on a long stalk anchored by a small holdfast, pumping water through six comb-like filters inside the cup. Its name means "gregarious", because it grew in dense meadows, sometimes with dozens of individuals together. Its crowded clusters make the colony very hard to wipe out, even though each animal is soft and defenceless.

A priapulid worm about 7 cm long from the Burgess Shale of Canada that lived inside a tough, slightly tapering tube open at both ends, set upright in the mud. From the top it shot out a spiny, turned-out proboscis to grab small animals passing by and pulled them down into its throat. Sheltered in its tube and quick to strike, it is a dangerous ambusher that is hard to hit back.

A freshwater shark up to about 3 metres long that ruled the lakes and rivers of the Late Carboniferous coal swamps of North America, about 305 million years ago. It had an eel-like body with a long ribbon of a dorsal fin, a broad head full of two-pronged teeth and a long, serrated spine sticking back from its skull. The top predator of its waters, it ate fish, amphibians and even smaller sharks, and its strong bite made it one of the most dangerous animals of its time.

A large, long-bodied embolomere about 3 metres long from Late Carboniferous coal swamps of Scotland and England, about 310 million years ago. Its big, deep skull carried some of the largest fangs of any early tetrapod, on the jaws and the roof of the mouth. It swam with eel-like waves of its long body and tall tail and seized fish and other amphibians with a crushing, piercing bite, though its long, lightly armoured body was vulnerable when attacked itself.

A heavy, crocodile-like baphetid early tetrapod about 1.5 to 2 metres long from the Late Carboniferous coal swamps of England, about 310 million years ago. Its name means 'big head': the broad, flat, thick-boned skull, about a third of a metre long, was lined with large fangs. It lay in wait at the water's edge on short, sturdy legs and lunged at fish and amphibians, and its massive skull and bulk made it hard to injure.

A large scorpion about 30 centimetres long from the Early Carboniferous of southern Scotland, about 340 million years ago. It had big, strong pincers and a long tail ending in a large venom bulb and sting. It may have hunted along the shores of lagoons and pools, perhaps even in the water, catching fish and other small animals. Its venomous sting made it a dangerous attacker, but its body was easily crushed by larger predators.

A shark up to about a metre long from the Early Carboniferous seas of North America, about 340 million years ago. Males carried a strange 'ironing board' on the back: a tall spine topped by a broad, flat brush covered, like the top of the head, with enlarged tooth-like denticles. It was a quick, agile hunter of fish and squid-like animals, and the brush may have been used for display or to look too big to swallow.

A giant sea scorpion from the Early Carboniferous of Scotland, about 335 million years ago, up to about 1.7 metres long and one of the heaviest arthropods that ever lived. It had a huge, rounded head shield, a very broad body and front legs fringed with long spines that raked small animals out of the mud. A fossil trackway shows that it could drag itself over land. Its thick, ornamented armour and great bulk made it very hard to kill, but it was slow and had a weak attack.

The largest brachiopod that ever lived, with a shell up to about 30 centimetres wide, from the warm, shallow Early Carboniferous seas of Europe, Asia and North Africa, about 335 million years ago. It lay on the sea floor in a huge, thick, strongly curved shell, much wider than long, and fed by filtering food particles from the water through the gaping front of its shell. Its massive shell made it almost impossible for predators to break.

A trigonotarbid arachnid about 2 centimetres long from the Late Carboniferous coal forests of England, about 310 million years ago. Like other trigonotarbids it looked like a spider but had no silk or venom. Its broad, flattened body was armoured with plates covered in coarse bumps, and the rear edge of its back carried a row of stout spines. It hunted smaller arthropods in the leaf litter, and its armour and spines made it a tough, prickly mouthful.

A heavily built diadectid about 1.5 metres long from the Late Carboniferous of Colorado, about 305 million years ago, and one of the earliest land vertebrates to eat plants. It had a short, deep head with broad, blunt cheek teeth for grinding tough leaves, a massive barrel-shaped body to digest them and short, stout legs. Its great bulk gave it plenty of staying power in a fight, but it was slow and had little to attack with.

One of the oldest known griffinflies, with a wingspan of about 32 centimetres, from the Late Carboniferous of Hagen-Vorhalle in Germany, about 320 million years ago. Like its giant relative Meganeura it had huge eyes, a strong thorax, four long veined wings and spiny legs that formed a basket for snatching prey in mid-air. A fast, agile aerial hunter of other flying insects, it struck hard but had a fragile body.

A small, lizard-like early reptile about 20 centimetres long from the Late Carboniferous of Ohio, about 307 million years ago. Its name means 'coal runner': it had long, slender legs and long toes ending in sharp, curved claws, and it is the oldest known reptile adapted for climbing. It darted over the ground and up tree trunks of the coal forest after insects, escaping danger with speed rather than strength.

A small relative of the ratfishes, about 40 centimetres long, from the Late Carboniferous seas of North America, about 305 million years ago. It had a short body, huge eyes and enormous wing-like pectoral fins set high on the shoulders, their leading edges armed with hooked denticles. It may have used these fins to burst out of the water and glide like a flying fish. Fast and hard to catch, it was easily hurt once caught.

A megasecopteran insect from the Late Carboniferous of Commentry in France, about 300 million years ago, with a wingspan of up to about 20 centimetres. Megasecopterans were relatives of the palaeodictyopterans: they had a piercing beak for sucking plant juices and two pairs of slender wings that could not be folded back. As its name suggests, Mischoptera had dark, almost black wings. It was a quick flier that relied on speed and numbers rather than defences.

A legless, snake-like amphibian about 70 centimetres long from the Late Carboniferous of Illinois and Ohio, about 307 million years ago. This aistopod had a tiny, lightly built skull and an extremely long, thin body made of a great many vertebrae, with no trace of limbs. It slid through the leaf litter and shallow water of the coal swamps, ambushing insects and other small animals with a quick strike.

A small, eel-like lysorophian amphibian about 30 centimetres long from the Late Carboniferous coal swamps of North America, about 307 million years ago. It had a long body, a small, sturdy head and tiny limbs. When its pools dried out it dug a burrow in the mud and lay curled up inside, waiting for the rains, and fossils of Brachydectes have been found still coiled in their burrows. Hidden underground it survived droughts and attacks that killed other animals.

A sea lily from the Early Carboniferous, about 340 million years ago, one of the crinoids that grew in great meadows on shallow sea floors, their skeletons later piling up into the Carboniferous Limestone of England. It held a smooth, bowl-shaped cup high on a long, slightly twisted stem and spread five branching, feathery arms to catch food particles from the current. Like other crinoids it could regrow lost arms, so it recovered quickly from damage.

A jellyfish about 10 to 15 centimetres across from the Late Carboniferous of Mazon Creek in Illinois, about 307 million years ago, where it is by far the most common fossil of the shallow coastal waters. Its domed bell had a long, curtain-like skirt of tissue hanging from its rim. It drifted in large swarms and probably caught small animals with stinging cells, making a soft but painful target for predators.

The Asian cousin of Tyrannosaurus, about 10 metres long and 5 tonnes, that ruled the river plains of Mongolia about 70 million years ago. Its massive skull carried banana-sized teeth for a bone-crushing bite, while its arms were the smallest, relative to its body, of any tyrannosaur. It hunted the giant sauropods and duck-billed dinosaurs that lived alongside it.

The largest known raptor, a feathered dromaeosaurid about 6 metres long and up to half a tonne, from Utah about 135 million years ago. Each foot carried a sickle claw some 24 cm long, and it was stockier and more powerful than its smaller relatives. A block of rock holding several Utahraptors of different ages suggests they may have hunted or gathered in groups.

A spinosaurid about 9 metres long that hunted along rivers and lagoons in England and Spain about 125 million years ago. It had a long, narrow, crocodile-like snout with almost 100 teeth and a huge 30 cm thumb claw, used like a gaff to hook fish. Scales of a large fish and the bones of a young Iguanodon were found in its stomach, so it hunted both in the water and on land.

An abelisaurid about 7 metres long, the top predator of Madagascar about 70 million years ago. It had a short, deep, thick-roofed skull with a single knob-like horn, tiny stubby arms and stocky legs; it probably clamped on to prey in a bulldog-like grip rather than slashing. Tooth marks on its own species' bones show that it was a cannibal, eating others of its kind as well as the sauropod Rapetosaurus.

A giant mosasaur about 12 metres long from the seas of the Netherlands about 67 million years ago. Its short, very deep and heavily built jaws were lined with thick, blunt-tipped teeth and extra teeth on the roof of the mouth, made for gripping and crushing hard prey. It cracked open sea turtles, ammonites and even other marine reptiles, and its skeletons carry healed wounds from fights.

A giant azhdarchid pterosaur from Hateg Island in what is now Romania, about 66 million years ago, with a wingspan of 10-12 metres. Unlike its slender relatives it had a short, very wide skull about 3 metres long and a thick, muscular neck. On an island without large predatory dinosaurs, it probably stalked the ground on all fours as the top predator, grabbing dwarf dinosaurs with its huge beak.

Nicknamed 'BoarCroc', a 6-metre crocodyliform from the Sahara of Niger about 95 million years ago. Three pairs of huge tusk-like teeth stuck out above and below its jaws like a boar's, and a bony ridge at the back of its head may have been used for ramming. Its long, upright legs and forward-facing eyes suggest it ran down prey on land, including small dinosaurs, rather than lurking in the water like a modern crocodile.

A tank-like ankylosaurid about 5.5 metres long and 2 tonnes from Alberta about 76 million years ago. Bands of bony plates and keeled spikes covered its neck, back and tail, and even its eyelids were armoured with bony shutters. Its stiff tail ended in a heavy club of fused bone that could smash the shins of an attacking tyrannosaur.

A nodosaur about 5.5 metres long and 1.3 tonnes from Alberta about 110 million years ago, known from a mummy-like fossil so well preserved that it looks like a sleeping statue. Its back was a mosaic of bony plates, and two long spikes jutted from its shoulders. Pigment traces show it was reddish-brown on top and paler below, a camouflage that suggests even this armoured giant needed to hide from predators.

A horned dinosaur about 5.5 metres long and 3 tonnes from Alberta about 75 million years ago. It had a single long nose horn up to 60 cm and a frill crowned with four to six long spikes, giving it one of the most spectacular heads of any dinosaur. Bonebeds of many individuals suggest it lived in herds, facing predators with a wall of horns.

One of the largest animals ever to walk the Earth, a titanosaur about 37 metres long and some 55-60 tonnes from Patagonia about 100 million years ago. It is known from the bones of at least six individuals, so its size is better established than that of most giant sauropods. Fully grown, it was simply too big for any predator to bring down, and its sheer bulk was its defence.

A small titanosaur about 12 metres long from Argentina about 70 million years ago, and the first sauropod found to have body armour. Its back was studded with bony plates up to 12 cm across set in a mosaic of small bony nodules. Females may have laid their eggs in huge nesting colonies, like those found nearby at Auca Mahuevo.

The largest known hadrosaur and the biggest ornithopod of all, about 15 metres long and some 13-16 tonnes, from the floodplains of Shandong in China about 72 million years ago. It had a long, flat, crestless head with a broad duck-bill and some 1,500 grinding teeth. It lived in large herds, and its great size made adults hard for even tyrannosaurs to bring down.

A giant sea turtle about 3 metres long from the inland sea of North America about 85 million years ago, second in size only to its relative Archelon. Its shell was reduced to a light frame of bone covered in leathery skin, like a modern leatherback's, and it swam with long, wing-like front flippers. It crushed jellyfish, squid and shelled molluscs with its broad beak, and buried large clutches of eggs on the beaches.

The largest well-known ostrich dinosaur, about 6 metres long and 400 kg, from Mongolia about 70 million years ago. It had a small toothless beak, large eyes, a long neck and very long legs built for speed, and may have run at 40-60 km/h. Many skeletons of different ages found together suggest it lived in groups, relying on speed rather than weapons to escape predators.

A short-necked polycotylid plesiosaur about 4.5 metres long from the inland sea of North America about 80 million years ago. Its long, slender jaws were lined with needle-like teeth for snapping up fast fish and squid, and its streamlined body and four long flippers made it one of the fastest swimmers of its time. Like its close relatives it gave birth to a single large live baby at sea instead of laying eggs.

A gull-sized seabird about 30 cm long with a 60 cm wingspan that flew over the inland sea of North America about 95-83 million years ago. It looked much like a tern but still had sharp, curved teeth in its jaws, a mix of ancient and modern features that made it a key link between dinosaurs and modern birds. A strong, fast flier, it nested in colonies and dived for fish.

A small, fast plant-eating dinosaur from the polar forests of southern Australia about 110 million years ago, when the region lay inside the Antarctic Circle and had weeks of winter darkness. Its tail was about three times as long as its body, perhaps wrapped around it for warmth, and its large eye sockets suggest keen sight in the long polar night. It relied on speed and agility to dodge predators.

The first known burrowing dinosaur, a small plant-eater about 2 metres long from Montana and Idaho about 95 million years ago. It was found curled up with two half-grown young at the end of a sloping, S-shaped burrow, the first evidence of a dinosaur digging dens and caring for its offspring. Its strong snout, shoulders and hips helped it dig, and a burrow offered shelter from predators and the weather.

Nicknamed the 'devil frog', one of the largest frogs ever, about 40 cm long and up to 4.5 kg, from Madagascar about 70 million years ago. Related to the modern South American horned frogs, it had a huge, wide mouth, powerful jaws and a bony shield on its skull. It was a sit-and-wait ambusher that could swallow lizards, small crocodiles and probably hatchling dinosaurs whole.

A duck-sized dromaeosaur relative about 60 cm long from Mongolia about 75 million years ago, with a long swan-like neck, a flat, toothy snout and flipper-like forelimbs. It probably lived like a merganser or a cormorant, walking upright on land and swimming after fish and small water animals. It is one of the very few non-bird dinosaurs thought to have hunted in the water.

The 'crow shark', a mackerel shark about 2-3 metres long that swarmed the seas of the Late Cretaceous about 100-70 million years ago. Its curved, finely serrated teeth, like small saws, were good for cutting chunks out of carcasses. Its tooth marks and embedded teeth have been found on mosasaurs, sea turtles and even a duck-billed dinosaur washed out to sea, showing that it fed on anything it could find, dead or alive.

One of the largest animals of the Late Devonian seas, about 370 million years ago: an armoured placoderm that may have reached 5 to 7 metres long. Despite its size and heavy head-and-shoulder armour, its long jaws were small-mouthed and toothless, and it probably cruised slowly through open water filtering out small prey, much like a basking shark. Its sheer bulk made it very hard for any predator to bring down.

A small, quick arthrodire placoderm about 25 centimetres long from a Late Devonian reef in Western Australia, about 380 million years ago. It had a streamlined armoured head and shoulder shield, large eyes and sharp, self-sharpening bony jaw blades, and darted about the reef snapping up small fish and shrimp-like prey. It is the official state fossil of Western Australia.

An early shark perhaps about a metre long from the Middle Devonian rivers and lakes of Antarctica and Australia, about 385 million years ago, and one of the first sharks to live in fresh water. It had a slender, rather eel-like body, a long, stout spine standing just behind its head and teeth with two large, diverging points, ideal for gripping slippery prey. It struck hard at other fish, but its thin skin gave it little protection.

A lobe-finned predator about a metre long from a Late Devonian reef in Western Australia, about 380 million years ago. At the front of its lower jaw stood whorls of huge, curved fangs that slotted into pits in the snout when it shut its mouth, giving it one of the most fearsome bites of its time for its size. It probably lurked in reef crevices and lunged out to impale passing fish.

A sleek lobe-finned hunter about 1.6 metres long from the Late Devonian rivers of New South Wales, Australia, about 365 million years ago. Torpedo-shaped, with its dorsal and anal fins set far back and a symmetrical tail, it was built for sudden bursts of speed like a modern pike or barracuda. It waited in ambush and shot forward to seize armoured fish in its long, fanged jaws, but its lightly built body could not take much punishment.

A lungfish about half a metre long from a Late Devonian reef in Western Australia, about 380 million years ago. Instead of the broad tooth plates of most lungfishes it had a long, flattened, duck-bill-like snout lined with small bony bumps, which it probably used to root about the reef and crush shelled animals. Its body was clad in thick, shiny bony scales that made it very hard to bite through, though it was a slow swimmer.

A four-limbed animal perhaps about a metre long from the very end of the Devonian in Russia, about 365 million years ago. It had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, and its sturdy limbs and shoulders suggest it moved on land better than Acanthostega or Ichthyostega. It lived around shallow coastal lagoons, hunting fish in the water and small animals along the shore.

A goniatite ammonoid from the Late Devonian seas, about 375 million years ago, so common around the world that it marks a whole stretch of geological time. Its tightly coiled, flattened shell, up to about 15 centimetres across, carried zig-zag suture lines and was more streamlined than those of earlier, loosely coiled ammonoids. It darted backwards by jet propulsion to snatch small prey or escape danger.

One of the largest trilobites ever, up to about 60 centimetres long, from the Middle Devonian seas of New York and Ontario, about 390 million years ago. It bristled from head to tail with spines and knobs: long spines on its cheeks, along every body segment and around its tail shield. This spiky armour made it a near-impossible mouthful even for the big armoured fish of its time, though it was slow and had little to fight back with.

A small, spectacularly spiny trilobite about 6 centimetres long from the Early Devonian seas of Morocco, about 400 million years ago. Two great curled horns like a ram's swept back from its head, and long paired spines bristled from its cheeks, every body segment and its tail.
