It was small and harmless, but its thicket of spines made it almost impossible to swallow.

A large sea scorpion well over a metre long from the Early Devonian rivers and lakes of Scotland, about 410 million years ago. Instead of swimming paddles it stalked along the bottom on long, stilt-like legs, the last pairs reaching far behind its body, and its body ended in a long, spike-like tail. Big and sturdy, it was hard for predators to tackle, though it moved slowly and fed on small animals it found in the mud.

A small scorpion only a few centimetres long from the Early Devonian seas of western Germany, about 400 million years ago. Rows of feathery, gill-like flaps along the sides of its body show that it lived and breathed under water, long after scorpions first appeared. Armed with grasping pincers and a venomous sting, it struck very hard for its size, but its slender body was fragile.

One of the oldest insects known, from the hot-spring wetlands of Rhynie in Scotland, about 410 million years ago. Only its tiny head has been found, but its strong, triangular, toothed jaws are like those of winged insects, hinting that insects may have taken to the air far earlier than their oldest known wings. Tiny and fragile but breeding in huge numbers, it would have swarmed among the first low land plants.

A radiodont, a relative of Anomalocaris, about 10 centimetres long from the Early Devonian seas of western Germany, about 400 million years ago, living long after almost all of its kind had died out. It had a big head with large eyes, a pair of spiny grasping arms and a ring-shaped mouth, and a single pair of large wing-like flaps that drove it swiftly through the water. A sharp-eyed ambusher that struck hard, it had only a soft, lightly built body to protect it.

The oldest known harvestman, from the hot-spring wetlands of Rhynie in Scotland, about 410 million years ago. It already looked remarkably like living harvestmen, with a compact oval body only a few millimetres long, a pair of eyes on a central bump and four pairs of very long, thin legs. Those stilt-like legs carried it quickly over the ground as it searched for small prey and decaying scraps.

A brittle star about 10 centimetres across from the Early Devonian seas of western Germany, about 400 million years ago, with a small central disc and five long, slender, snake-like arms. It crawled over the muddy seafloor picking up scraps of food with its flexible arms. Like living brittle stars it could probably shed an arm to escape a predator and grow it back, which made it extremely hard to kill off.

A stalked, branching polyp about 20 cm tall whose two cups each held a crown of stinging tentacles, its name meaning "Attenborough's dawn lantern". Living about 560 million years ago in a deep sea otherwise full of passive fronds, it is one of the oldest known predatory animals, an early relative of jellyfish that snared passing prey. Its stinging cells make it the deadliest attacker of its world, but its thin skeleton and soft polyps break easily.

A square-bodied polyp a few centimetres across, held up on a short stalk from a disc in the mud, with four corner arms that split into bunches of tentacles. About 560 million years old, it shows the oldest known muscle tissue, bundles of fibres running through its body, and looks much like a living stalked jellyfish. Those muscles let it fold its arms quickly round prey and pull back from attackers.

A round, many-ringed disc up to about 8 cm across, fringed with a crowd of short radiating tentacles, from the Ediacaran of South Australia. It was first taken for a floating colony like the living blue button Porpita, sailing with the currents and stinging small animals beneath it, though some think it was a polyp fixed to the seabed. Riding the water lets it spread quickly, but its soft body has no protection at all.

One of the first animals to build a hard skeleton: a lumpy crust up to a metre across that filled cracks in the reefs of what is now Namibia about 548 million years ago. Its body was a maze of thin mineral walls and channels, probably a sponge or a coral-like animal straining food from the water. Huge, rooted and almost all skeleton, it can soak up enormous damage, but it cannot move or strike back.

A slender, four-sided tube a few centimetres long, built of overlapping rings of small hardened plates, from the last Ediacaran seas of Brazil, Paraguay and the western United States. The polyp inside, probably an early relative of jellyfish, reached out of the open top to catch food and drew back in when threatened. Its jointed armour is among the oldest animal skeletons, making it very hard to crack, though it has little to fight back with.

A sack-shaped animal 5 to 10 cm tall from Namibia, about 548 million years old, whose wall was a quilt of tubes sewn together along a zigzag seam. It lived half buried in sand, often in crowded patches, with only its open rim above the seabed, where its shape steered currents and food into the cup. Anchored in sand, with a tough padded body and neighbours sheltering it, it is very hard to dig out, but it has no way to attack.

A long, narrow, segmented animal up to 27 cm long, each of its fifty or so body units ending in a pair of backward-pointing lobes, from 550-million-year-old rocks in the Yangtze Gorges of China. Some fossils end at the tip of the trail they left, proving it moved by itself and is one of the oldest mobile animals with a segmented body. One of the most active animals of its day, it roams the seabed quickly, but it is soft and unarmed.

A flat, oval animal up to about 8 cm long from the White Sea coast of Russia, about 555 million years old, with a smooth shield-like front and rows of offset segments behind it. Like its relatives Dickinsonia and Yorgia it glided over the microbial mats that covered the seabed, digesting them through its underside and moving on. It roams quickly from mat to mat, but its thin body offers little protection.

A thin, hook-curved worm a few centimetres long from the Ediacaran of South Australia, described in 2024 as the oldest known relative of the roundworms, arthropods and their kin. It burrowed through the sand just under the microbial mat, leaving long winding tunnels that are found alongside its fossils. Hidden in its burrow it is hard to find and hit, though it is frail once caught.

A small ring-shaped animal 0.5 to 2 cm across with raised spiral ridges, named after Barack Obama and found in dense clusters in 550-million-year-old rocks of South Australia. It sat partly sunk into the tough microbial mat on the seabed, and nothing quite like it is known from any other time. Its stiff, embedded ring is hard to dislodge, and its crowded beds quickly fill the space around it, but it cannot attack.

One of the largest land predators of the Late Jurassic, a heavily built megalosaurid about 9-10 metres long from western North America. Its long, deep skull held long, serrated, blade-like teeth, and its short arms were unusually powerful, with big thumb claws. It could tackle sauropods and stegosaurs, but its bulk made it slower than lighter hunters.

A giant pliosaur from the Late Jurassic seas around Svalbard, about 150 million years ago, nicknamed 'Predator X'. It reached perhaps 10-12 metres, with a skull around 2 metres long and one of the strongest bites of any known animal. Driven by four huge flippers, it ambushed ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs and large fish, crushing them in jaws lined with massive ridged teeth.

The largest of the teleosaurids, marine relatives of crocodiles, reaching about 7 metres in the coastal seas and lagoons of Late Jurassic Europe. Its broad, robust snout carried short, blunt teeth built to crack turtle shells and hard-bodied prey. Unlike the smooth-skinned metriorhynchids, it kept thick rows of bony armour on its back and belly, making it both a crushing biter and hard to wound.

One of the largest Early Jurassic ichthyosaurs, up to about 9 metres long, from the seas of England and Germany around 195 million years ago. Its eyes were about 25 cm across, among the largest of any animal ever, letting it hunt in dim, deep water. A fast, dolphin-shaped swimmer with a long toothed snout, it was the top predator of its seas and even fed on other ichthyosaurs, though its slim body had little protection.

A large Jurassic relative of today's ratfish, about 1.5 metres long, that lived in the shallow seas of Europe. Beak-like tooth plates let it crush clams, snails and crustaceans on the sea floor. In front of its tall first dorsal fin stood a long, serrated spine; in living chimaeras such spines carry venom, making the fish a painful mouthful for predators.

A low-slung stegosaur about 4.2 metres long from the Late Jurassic of Sichuan, China. It is named for the enormous spikes that swept back from its shoulders, each almost twice as long as its shoulder blade, which shielded its flanks from biting predators. Small plates ran down its back, and its tail ended in two pairs of spikes.

One of the earliest true ankylosaurs, about 3-4 metres long, from the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of Wyoming. Its low, broad body was covered from neck to tail in rows of conical bony osteoderms, with longer spikes along its flanks and a heavily armoured skull. It had no tail club, so it relied almost entirely on its armour, crouching low so predators could not reach its soft belly.

A diplodocid sauropod from the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of Colorado and Wyoming, and one of the longest dinosaurs known, at roughly 33-35 metres from snout to tail tip. Its immensely long neck let it browse over a huge area without moving, and its whip-like tail could be lashed at attackers. Its sheer size meant that a full-grown adult had almost nothing to fear, though it was slow and needed vast amounts of food.

A relatively small, short-necked sauropod about 9-10 metres long from the Middle Jurassic of Sichuan, China, known from many complete skeletons. Its tail ended in a bony club armed with short spikes, a weapon it could swing at predators. It browsed on low vegetation and probably lived in herds.

One of the oldest turtles from North America, a small freshwater turtle from the Early Jurassic of Arizona, about 190 million years ago. Its low, smooth shell had lost the spikes of earlier turtles, and it lived in streams and pools, feeding on small animals and plants. Safe inside its shell from most attackers, it was slow on land and had a weak bite.

A pterosaur with a wingspan of about 0.9 metres from the Middle to Late Jurassic forests of north-eastern China, about 160 million years ago. It combined the long tail of early pterosaurs with the long skull and neck of later ones, a mix that made it famous as a transitional form. A fast, agile flier, it snatched small animals, perhaps including small feathered dinosaurs, with its toothed jaws. One fossil female was preserved with an egg.

A tiny, frog-faced pterosaur from the Late Jurassic Solnhofen lagoons of Bavaria, with a wingspan of about 35-50 cm and only a stub of a tail. Its short, broad head had large eyes and a wide mouth of small peg teeth, and its body was covered in fuzzy fibres. It was a nimble aerial insect-hunter, probably active at dusk, and too quick and small to be easily caught.

A slender, fast-running ornithopod about 3 metres long from the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of the western United States. Its long, powerful hind legs, with very long shins, made it one of the fastest dinosaurs of its time, and it relied on speed rather than armour to escape predators such as Allosaurus. It cropped plants with a horny beak and ground them with ridged cheek teeth.

A small, fast ornithischian dinosaur about 1.2 metres long from the Early Jurassic of South Africa, about 200 million years ago. Its name means 'different-toothed lizard': it had a horny beak, chisel-like cheek teeth for chopping plants and a pair of long, fang-like tusks used for display, fighting or eating small animals. Its strong, grasping hands could dig up roots or catch prey, making it quick and surprisingly well armed for its size.

A tiny, mole-like docodont, a close relative of true mammals, about 9 cm long and weighing under 20 grams, from the Jurassic forests of northern China about 160 million years ago. Its broad, spade-like hands, with shortened fingers and big claws, were built for digging, much like those of today's golden moles. It spent most of its life underground hunting worms and insect grubs, where few predators could reach it.

A giant early flea from the Middle Jurassic of north-eastern China, about 165 million years ago; females reached about 2 cm, many times the size of modern fleas. It was wingless and flattened, with long legs ending in strong claws for clinging to its host and a long, saw-edged mouthpart for piercing thick skin. It probably fed on the blood of feathered dinosaurs, pterosaurs and early mammals, and could not jump like living fleas.

A lion-sized 'false sabre-tooth' of Late Miocene North America, about 9 million years ago, with the longest upper canines for its skull size of any cat-like predator, sheathed by a deep bony flange on the lower jaw. Its short, massively muscled legs were made for ambush, not chases: it wrestled big prey such as rhinos and camels to the ground and killed with a slashing bite. Few animals of its time could survive its first strike.

A giant hyaenodont of Early Miocene East Africa, about 22 million years ago, perhaps heavier than a polar bear and one of the largest meat-eating land mammals ever. It came from an old line of predators unrelated to cats, despite its name meaning 'big lion' in Swahili, and had a huge skull with long, scissor-like cheek teeth. Strong enough to tackle early elephants and rhinos, it was slow and heavy on its short legs.

A giant viper from the Pliocene of northern Greece, about 4 million years ago, and probably the largest venomous snake that ever lived, perhaps 3 to 4 metres long and over 20 kilograms. Like today's heavy-bodied vipers it most likely lay in wait and struck with long, folding fangs, injecting a large dose of venom. Its bite was deadly, but it was slow and had no armour.

The largest hyena that ever lived, about lion-sized at up to 110 kg, ranging across Africa and Eurasia from the Late Pliocene to the Middle Pleistocene. Its short, broad muzzle and huge teeth gave it a bone-cracking bite, and it probably stole kills from sabre-toothed cats as well as hunting for itself. It lived and fought in clans.

A giant otter about the size of a lion, weighing perhaps 200 kg, from the Early Pliocene of Ethiopia some 3.5 million years ago. Its huge, rounded cheek teeth could crush shells, bones and turtle shells, and chemical traces in its teeth suggest it hunted on land as much as in the water. It was one of the largest members of the weasel family ever.

The largest land tortoise known, with a shell about 2 metres long, living from Pakistan and India to Southeast Asia from the Late Miocene to the Pleistocene. It plodded on elephant-like legs, browsing low plants, and when threatened it could draw its scaly limbs and head in under a domed shell that almost no predator could break. It was extremely slow.

A glyptodont that walked north across the newly formed land bridge of Panama about 3 million years ago and spread into the southern United States. This car-sized armadillo relative, about 2.5 m long, was covered by a rigid domed shell of hundreds of fused bony plates, with a bony cap on its head and rings of armour on its tail. It grazed in wet grasslands and marshes, and its shell made it nearly immune to the big cats and terror birds of its day.

A Miocene armadillo of Patagonia, about a metre long, with a pair of tall, horn-like armour scales on its snout, the only armadillo known to have had horns. Its body was covered by flexible bands of bony plates and its head by a bony shield. Once thought to be a meat-eater, it probably dug for roots and tubers, relying on its armour and horns against predators.

The largest rodent ever found, a bull-sized relative of the pacarana from the Pliocene of Uruguay, about 3 m long and perhaps half a tonne to a tonne in weight. It lived in the forested deltas of the ancient Rio de la Plata, feeding on soft plants. Its enormous incisors could bite as hard as a tiger's, for digging and for fighting off predators, and its sheer bulk made it very hard to kill.

A cheetah of Pliocene and Early Pleistocene Europe, Asia and Africa, about twice as heavy as the living cheetah and nearly as big as a lion. Long, slender legs, a flexible spine and claws that stayed partly out for grip made it a sprinter that could run down antelopes and horses in open country. Built for speed rather than fighting, it was easily hurt and could lose its kills to hyenas.

A small, lightly built hoofed mammal of Miocene Patagonia, about 70 cm long, belonging to the litopterns, a South American group unrelated to horses. It evolved a single-toed foot even more reduced than a modern horse's, with the side toes shrunk to tiny splints. It was fast and nimble on its long, thin legs, but small and defenceless if caught.

A large, mako-like shark of Miocene and Pliocene seas, up to about 6 m long, now thought to be the direct ancestor of the great white shark. Its broad, flat, smooth-edged teeth sliced through blubber and flesh, and fossil whale bones with its bite marks show that it hunted small baleen whales. Warm-bodied and streamlined, it was one of the fastest big predators in the sea, though far lighter than Megalodon.

A large seal-like pinniped of the Middle Miocene North Pacific, about 15 million years ago, with males reaching about 2.5 m. It had huge eyes for hunting fish and squid in dim water, a long neck and big flippers, and was fast and agile in the water. Males were much bigger than females and probably fought over harems on beaches, like modern sea lions.

A giant salamander up to about 2.3 m long from the Miocene and Pliocene rivers of North America, a close relative of today's Chinese and Japanese giant salamanders. It lay in wait on stream beds and snapped up fish, crayfish and frogs with a sudden gulp of its broad, flat head. Like its living relatives it breathed partly through its loose, wrinkled skin and could regrow lost toes and parts of limbs, which made it hard to wear down.

A huge caiman of Late Miocene South American wetlands, perhaps 8 to 10 m long, with a long, flat, broad 'duck-billed' skull lined with many small teeth. Its weak jaws were poorly suited to fighting large prey, so it probably gulped mouthfuls of water and strained out fish and small animals, like a pelican. Its heavy armour of bony scutes and its great bulk still made it a hard target.

A New World army ant preserved in Miocene amber from the Dominican Republic, about 20 million years old, the first fossil army ant ever described. Like its living relatives it was almost blind and had no permanent nest: colonies of hundreds of thousands moved camp again and again, sending out raiding columns that overwhelmed other ants, insects and small animals by sheer numbers. Each worker was tiny, but a raid could strip the forest floor of prey.

A big straight-shelled nautiloid from the Middle and Late Ordovician seas of North America, with a heavy, spindle-shaped shell up to about a metre long. A broad, bead-like tube loaded with mineral deposits ran down the middle of the shell as ballast, so it swam slowly and kept close to the sea floor. Its strong arms and beak made it one of the hardest-hitting predators of its time, able to tear apart trilobites and other armoured prey.

The commonest cephalopod of the Early and Middle Ordovician seas of Baltica, so abundant that a Scandinavian limestone was once named after it. An endocerid, it had a long, smooth, straight shell probably a metre or more long, with a wide tube along the belly filled with stacked cone-shaped deposits that acted as ballast. Big, heavily built and hard to kill, it cruised slowly over the sea floor hunting trilobites and other prey.

An odd nautiloid from the Middle Ordovician of North America whose straight shell was squashed flat: several times wider than high, with an arched back, a flat belly and sharp, keel-like edges, like a long, flattened spearhead. It probably lay still on the sea floor, its low, broad shell blending into the bottom, and ambushed trilobites and worms that came too close. Its flat shape made it hard to spot and hard to flip over.

A sea scorpion about 45 cm long from the Late Ordovician of New York State, a close relative of Megalograptus. Its name means 'spiny jaw': its front limbs bristled with long, sharp, paired spines for seizing prey and holding it to the mouth. Heavily armed and quick to strike, it was one of the most dangerous hunters of its sea floor, though its thin armour left it vulnerable.

A streamlined, torpedo-shaped trilobite up to about 10 cm long from the Middle Ordovician of Bohemia and Iberia. Its long, smooth, highly arched shield had no spines, and very large eyes wrapped round the sides of its head. Unlike most trilobites it lived in open water as a fast-swimming hunter of small animals, but its light shell made it fragile in a fight.

A giant predatory conodont from the Middle Ordovician of Iowa, about 460 million years ago, known from complete feeding apparatuses of fifteen tooth-like elements up to 1.6 cm long, huge for a conodont. Its soft body is unknown, but it was probably an eel-like swimmer much larger than most of its relatives. A fast, active hunter of open water, it could tackle bigger prey than other conodonts but had no armour to protect it.

A small, slender conodont a few centimetres long; Panderodus was one of the longest-lived and most widespread conodonts. Its flattened, eel-like body carried a grasping apparatus of long, slender, fang-like cones, each with a deep groove along its side that may have carried venom, which would make it one of the oldest venomous animals known. Tiny and fragile but quick, it could subdue prey far tougher than itself.

One of the oldest armoured fish, a jawless vertebrate from the Late Ordovician coastal seas of Colorado, about 455 million years ago. Its head was encased in a shield of many small bony plates carved with fine ridges, and inside lay one of the oldest known cartilage braincases. Slow and toothless, it fed on small particles near the bottom, trusting its heavy armour to protect it.

One of the largest trilobites that ever lived, from the Middle Ordovician of Portugal, Spain and Bohemia: complete shields over 40 cm long are known, and some may have reached 60 cm or more. Its broad, flat, oval body had short cheek spines and a big, wide tail shield. It lived in cool, muddy seas on the edge of the southern supercontinent Gondwana, and its sheer size made it very hard for predators to kill.

Perhaps the spiniest of all trilobites, from the Middle Ordovician of the St Petersburg region of Russia. Its small, flat body was ringed with long, slender spines growing from its cheeks, every body segment and its tail, and a pair of very long spines rose from the back of its head and swept back over its body. The spines made it a painful mouthful for any predator, but it was a slow crawler with little bite of its own.

A smooth, rounded trilobite a few centimetres long from the Late Ordovician of eastern North America. Its head and tail shields were very strongly arched and almost featureless, and its small eyes sat far back on the head. It probably spent most of its life sitting in a burrow with only the front of its head showing, feeding on particles in the water; tucked into the sediment it was very hard for predators to dig out.

A large, heavy sea snail from the Middle Ordovician of North America, several centimetres to more than 8 cm across, with a thick shell coiled almost flat. Its foot carried a very thick, horn-shaped lid of shell that sealed the big opening like a trapdoor and may also have anchored the snail to the bottom. Shut inside, it was nearly impossible to crack, though it could do little more than graze and wait.

An unusual 'cystoid' echinoderm a few centimetres long from the Late Ordovician of Britain and North America. Unlike most of its relatives it was not fixed to the sea floor: its flattened, plated body lay on the mud, with two long feeding arms reaching forward and a flexible, muscular stem behind that it probably used to push itself along. Low and armour-plated, it was an awkward target for predators as it crept about picking up food from the mud.

A conulariid from the Late Ordovician seas of Ontario, Quebec and New York, a relative of jellyfish that lived in a tall, slender, four-sided pyramid of thin, flexible skeleton several centimetres long, finely ribbed across each face. Its narrow end was attached to a shell or the sea floor, and from the wide end it probably spread a crown of stinging tentacles to catch passing prey. When threatened it could fold four triangular flaps shut over the opening.

The only large Ordovician horn coral, common in the Late Ordovician seas of Kentucky, Indiana, Ohio and Ontario. Each polyp lived alone in a thick, curved, cone-shaped skeleton usually 4-8 cm and up to 13 cm long, lying on the soft sea floor; its deep cup was lined with many crowded ridges whose inner ends twisted together into a raised knot in the middle. Its heavy skeleton made it very hard to damage, and old shells often became homes for encrusting bryozoans.

An armoured worm a few centimetres long from the Early Ordovician of Morocco, one of the machaeridians, a long-puzzling group now known to be annelids related to today's scaleworms. Its back was covered from end to end by rows of overlapping, ridged calcite plates like roof tiles, with bristly paddle-like legs and a pair of small jaws beneath. It crawled over and into the sea-floor mud, and most small predators could not bite through its plates.

One of the largest terror birds of the Oligocene of Patagonia, a flightless predator about 2 m tall. It was heavier and slower than its lanky later relatives, but its huge, deep, hooked beak could split open prey with downward hatchet blows. Its beak strike was among the hardest blows of any Paleogene hunter, but it had little to protect itself in a drawn-out fight.

A giant oxyaenid from the late Eocene of Mongolia, a bear-sized and bear-shaped meat-eater about 3 m long that may have weighed 800 kg. Its broad skull held huge canines and blunt, crushing cheek teeth that could crack bones and turtle shells. Its bite was devastating, but it walked flat-footed on short legs and could not chase down fast prey.

An early electric ray from the Eocene seas of northern Italy, about half a metre long. Its round, soft disc held two large electric organs that could stun fish with a powerful shock, so it could swallow them whole. It lay half buried in the sand to ambush prey; the shock was its only weapon, as its flabby body had no armour.

A land-hunting crocodylian about 3 m long from the Eocene forests of Germany, nicknamed the hoofed crocodile. It stood tall on long, upright legs with blunt, hoof-like claws, and its deep, narrow snout bore blade-like serrated teeth for slicing flesh. It could run down early horses and other mammals on land, far from the water.

A huge brontothere from the late Eocene of Mongolia, about 2.5 m at the shoulder. Instead of a forked horn, its nasal bones rose into a single tall, broad bony shield above the snout, used like a battering ram. Massive and thick-skinned, it could shrug off most attacks, but it was slow and fed only on soft plants.

A colossal early whale from the middle Eocene of Peru, about 17-20 m long and possibly the heaviest animal that ever lived. Its ribs and backbone were enormously thickened and dense, ballast for a slow life in shallow coastal water, where it probably fed on the sea floor. Its sheer bulk made it almost impossible to kill, but it was a slow, gentle giant.

A giant side-necked turtle from the Paleocene swamp forests of Colombia, with a shell about 1.7 m long. It shared its rivers with Titanoboa, and its huge head and powerful jaws were big enough to eat crocodile-sized prey. Its massive shell made it one of the best-armoured animals of its age, though it moved slowly.

One of the earliest giant indricotheres, a hornless rhinoceros from the late Eocene and early Oligocene of China and Mongolia, close in size to Paraceratherium. Long, pillar-like legs and a long neck let it browse treetops, and unlike its later relatives it kept a full set of front teeth. Its enormous size gave it huge stamina in a fight, but it had no horns and moved slowly.

A giant bony-toothed bird from the early Eocene coasts of England, with long, narrow wings spanning perhaps 4-5 m. Like a huge albatross it glided for days over the open sea, snatching fish and squid with a long bill lined with sharp bony spikes. It covered vast distances with ease, but its hollow bones made it fragile.

Nordenskjoeld's giant penguin, from the late Eocene of Antarctica, stood about 1.7 m tall and weighed some 90 kg, one of the largest penguins ever. Its wings were stiff flippers with a slight bend at the elbow, driving it through the water at speed after fish and squid. It was a fast, agile swimmer but no fighter.

A running rhinoceros from the late Eocene and Oligocene of North America, hornless and about the size of a pony. Its long, slender legs ended in three-toed hooves, built for speed across open plains. It escaped danger by outrunning it rather than fighting.

A giant sea snake from the Eocene seaway that once crossed the Sahara, perhaps 8 m long, one of the longest snakes known. Its long, muscular body was flattened from side to side toward the tail into a swimming paddle. It lay in wait in warm, shallow coastal water and seized fish and other prey with a sudden lunge.

The largest ant known, from the warm early Eocene forests of Germany; its winged queens were about 6 cm long with a 15 cm wingspan, as big as a hummingbird. It lived only where the climate was tropical. Each ant was weak, but huge colonies swarmed over prey and rivals together.

A small burrowing palaeanodont from the Oligocene of North America, about 20 cm long and a distant relative of pangolins. Built like a golden mole, it had a shovel-like snout, tiny eyes and huge claws on its short forelimbs for tunnelling through loose sand after ants and termites. Hidden underground, it was very hard for predators to reach.

A crocodile newt about 15-20 cm long from the late Oligocene and Miocene lakes of Europe. Its skin was rough and warty, with rows of knobs along the back and the sharp tips of its ribs along each flank, which in living relatives can pierce the skin to inject toxic secretions. Weak in attack, it was a painful, poisonous mouthful for any predator.

One of the largest African gorgonopsians, about 3 metres long, from the Late Permian of South Africa around 255 million years ago. Its skull was extraordinarily broad and heavy, with flaring cheek bones, rough bony bosses and huge sabre-like upper canines driven by powerful jaw muscles. It delivered some of the most devastating bites of its time and could tackle large dicynodonts and pareiasaurs. Its bulk made it strong but not especially quick.

A small, lightly built gorgonopsian about 1 metre long from the Late Permian of South Africa, around 255 million years ago; its name means 'wolf face'. It had long, slender, nearly upright legs, a narrow snout and long sabre-like canines. One of the most agile land predators of the Permian, it ran down small dicynodonts and other small animals, but its light build left it fragile in a fight.

A large predatory dinocephalian about 2.5 metres long from the Middle Permian of the Ural region of Russia, around 265 million years ago; its name means 'titanic murderer'. Its long, deep skull carried big interlocking front teeth for gripping and large canines for tearing, and its heavy body rested on strong, sprawling limbs. It was one of the top predators of its time, able to overpower large plant-eaters.

A small therocephalian about 45 centimetres long from the Late Permian of South Africa, around 256 million years ago. Its short, broad skull had a deep pit in front of each eye, linked to its long, ridged canines, which many scientists think held a venom gland. If so, it is the oldest known venomous four-legged animal, able to subdue prey far larger than its size would suggest. Its small, lightly built body offered little protection.

The largest amphibian known, perhaps 5.5 to 9 metres long, from the Early Permian rivers and lakes of north-eastern Brazil, around 275 million years ago. It looked much like a giant gharial, with an extremely long, narrow snout lined with sharp teeth, a long, low body and a powerful swimming tail. It lay in wait in the water and snapped up fish and other animals with a sideways sweep of its jaws. Its sheer size made it both a deadly ambusher and very hard to kill.

A cartilaginous fish from the Late Permian seas of East Greenland, around 258 million years ago, probably about 3 metres long and a relative of Helicoprion. Its name means 'flesh saw': the front of its lower jaw held a tall, curved whorl of big, blade-like triangular teeth that sliced against the upper jaw. Sleek and streamlined, it was a fast open-water hunter of fish and squid-like cephalopods. Like Helicoprion, it was more closely related to ratfishes than to true sharks.

A sail-backed sphenacodont about 2 metres long from the Early Permian of Texas, around 280 million years ago, and a close relative of Dimetrodon. It carried a tall sail on long spines along its back, but its snout was strikingly long, low and narrow, earning it the nickname 'fox-faced Dimetrodon'. Its slender jaws and blade-like teeth were probably used to snatch small animals out of burrows and crevices with quick, precise bites.

A small pareiasaur, only about 60 centimetres long, from the Late Permian of northern Scotland, around 255 million years ago. Its compact, armoured body was studded with bony knobs, and its head bristled with the most elaborate set of horns and spikes of any pareiasaur, including a pair of long horns at the back of the skull. A slow plant-eater, it relied on this spiky armour rather than speed, which made it a very painful mouthful for any predator.

A cow-sized pareiasaur about 2 metres long from the Late Permian of Niger, around 255 million years ago, when the region lay in the dry heart of the supercontinent Pangaea. Its name means 'knobby roof': its skull was covered with big, rounded bony bulges, and its heavy body was clad in bony armour. Unusually for a pareiasaur, it held its legs fairly upright beneath the body. Massive, armoured and hardy in the desert heat, it was very hard to bring down.

One of the largest dicynodonts of the Late Permian, about 2 metres long, from South Africa around 256 million years ago. It had a very broad, heavy skull with a toothless horny beak, a pair of tusks and big, rough bosses on the snout, possibly used in shoving contests between rivals. Its massive, barrel-shaped body gave it great staying power, letting it absorb punishment that would kill smaller plant-eaters.

A massive plant-eating dinocephalian about 3 metres long and weighing perhaps 1.5 to 2 tonnes, from the Middle Permian of South Africa around 263 million years ago. The roof of its skull was thickened into a broad bony dome up to 10 centimetres thick, which it probably used in head-butting contests. Its heavy, deep-chested body and armoured head made it a formidable opponent, though it was slow-moving.

A stocky, land-living amphibian about 40 centimetres long from the Early Permian of Texas and Oklahoma, around 280 million years ago. It had a large, broad head with big eyes and a large ear notch, and a double row of interlocking bony plates ran down its back like a shield. Better armoured than almost any other amphibian of its size, it hunted insects and small animals on land and was tough for predators to crack.

A gliding reptile about 40 centimetres long from the Late Permian of Germany, around 256 million years ago, named after Glaurung, the first of the dragons in Tolkien's tales. Long rods of bone growing from its flanks supported skin wings that let it glide swiftly from tree to tree, and the back of its skull bore a broad frill of spikes. It hunted insects in the trees and escaped danger by launching into the air, but its delicate body could not take much punishment.

A small palaeodictyopteran insect from the Early Permian of Kansas, around 275 million years ago, with a wingspan of only a few centimetres. Its four broad wings, held straight out like those of a dragonfly, were boldly crossed by dark bands, and it used a sharp, beak-like mouth to pierce plants and suck their sap. Agile in the air and breeding in great numbers, it survived by flying off and swarming rather than by fighting.

A small reptile about 25 centimetres long from the Early Permian of central Germany, around 290 million years ago, and the oldest known animal able to run on two legs. Its hind legs were much longer than its arms and it ran on its toes, holding its long tail out behind as a counterbalance. A plant-eater, it escaped predators by sprinting away on its hind legs, but it was too small and frail to fight back.

An aquatic reptile about 60 centimetres long from the Late Permian lakes of Madagascar, around 255 million years ago. Nearly two thirds of its length was a long, deep, flattened tail that it swung from side to side to swim, and it swallowed small stones that acted as ballast. A quick, agile swimmer, it chased small fish and other small water animals, but its slim body was easily hurt.

A small, mole-like dicynodont about 30 centimetres long from the Late Permian of South Africa, Zambia and India, around 256 million years ago. Its flat, wedge-shaped head and short, massively built forelimbs with broad claws were made for digging, and it probably spent much of its life underground like a modern mole, feeding on roots and perhaps insects. Hidden in its burrows it was hard for predators to reach, but in the open it was slow and clumsy.

A small, lizard-like reptile about 25 centimetres long from the Early Permian of Texas and Oklahoma, around 285 million years ago. Its broad head held several rows of teeth for crushing insects and tough plant food. It is one of the earliest animals known to shed its tail when grabbed by a predator, along weak planes in the tail bones, and then regrow it. This trick let it survive attacks that would kill most small animals.

The largest glyptodont, about 3.6 m long and up to 1.5 tonnes, from Pleistocene South America; it died out about 11,000 years ago. Its tall domed shell of fused bony plates was nearly impossible to bite through, and its long armoured tail ended in a massive club studded with spikes. Cracked shells of other Doedicurus suggest rivals clubbed each other, and a blow could break a predator's bones.

Often called the most venomous animal in the world, a nearly transparent box jellyfish of the coastal waters of northern Australia and Southeast Asia, with a bell up to 30 cm across and up to 15 tentacles, each up to 3 m long, trailing from each of its four corners. Millions of stinging cells inject a venom that can stop a human heart within minutes. Unlike most jellyfish it swims actively and steers with 24 eyes, some of them with lenses.

A cone snail of Indo-Pacific coral reefs, up to about 15 cm long, with a thin shell marked with a fine net pattern. At night it spreads its mouth like a net over small fish and stabs them with a hollow, harpoon-like tooth that injects a venom made of hundreds of different toxins, paralysing them almost instantly. It is the most dangerous cone snail to humans and has killed dozens of people who picked one up.

A stocky, black-and-silver member of the weasel family from Africa, the Middle East and India, about 75 cm long and famous for its fearlessness. Its thick, rubbery, loose skin resists bee stings, porcupine quills and teeth and lets it twist round to bite an attacker that has grabbed it, and it is partly resistant to snake venom. It digs out rodents, raids beehives, kills cobras and will stand up to lions and leopards.

The fastest land animal of the Americas, a deer-sized runner of the western prairies and deserts that can sprint at about 90 km/h and keep up 50 to 70 km/h for several kilometres. It is the last survivor of a family once rich in species and not a true antelope; its forked horn sheaths are shed every year. Its huge eyes spot danger kilometres away, and its speed may have evolved to escape the cheetah-like cats of Ice Age North America.

The largest pangolin, up to about 1.8 m long with its tail and over 30 kg, living in the forests and savannas of equatorial Africa. Its body is covered in large, overlapping scales of keratin, and when attacked it rolls into a tight ball that even lions struggle to open. At night it tears into termite mounds and ant nests with its huge front claws and licks up the insects with a very long, sticky tongue.

One of the giant sea scorpions, about 1.6 m long, from the Late Silurian and Early Devonian of Britain. In front of its small head shield it carried a pair of enormous, toothed pincers that could reach far forward, and its big compound eyes gave it sharp vision. Paddle-like hind legs and a broad, flat tail fin made it an active hunter that seized fish and other sea scorpions, the most powerful predator of its seas.

A sea scorpion about 90 cm long from the Late Silurian of Indiana, with a broad, flattened, almost round body and a narrow, rounded tail ending in a long spike. Its strong front legs pointed forward and bristled with long, curved spines, forming a cage to trap prey. It was probably a slow ambush hunter that waited on the sea floor and snatched animals that came too close.

A slender sea scorpion about 70 cm long from the Silurian of Scotland, a lighter relative of Pterygotus. It had long, thin pincers with small curved teeth, big eyes, broad swimming paddles and a wide, flat tail fin split into two lobes at its tip. Built for speed rather than strength, it chased small fish through open water but had only a thin shell.

One of the oldest known scorpions, about 2.5 cm long, from the Early Silurian of Wisconsin, about 437 million years ago. It already had grasping pincers, large eyes and a curled tail ending in a sting, and its heart and blood vessels were arranged much like those of living scorpions. It probably hunted small animals in shallow water and at the shoreline. Tiny and fragile, it packed a dangerous sting for its size.

An early relative of horseshoe crabs, a few centimetres long, from the Late Silurian. Its broad, crescent-shaped head shield was vaulted and covered with radiating ridges and bumps, and its segmented body tapered into a narrow tail with a spike. It probably ploughed through soft mud like a horseshoe crab, hiding under the sediment and grabbing worms and other small animals.

One of the largest Silurian trilobites, up to about 18 cm long, from the Rochester Shale of New York. Its very broad, flat shell was covered in tubercles, with a large swollen glabella, thorax segments drawn out into flat spines and a big tail shield fringed with broad spines. Slow-moving and heavily armoured, it fed on organic debris on the sea floor and was a hard, spiny mouthful for any predator.

A strange trilobite about 3 cm long from the mid-Silurian of Bohemia and Britain. Its head was little more than a huge, balloon-like glabella with long, outward-curving cheek spines, and its narrow body bore long, free spines along each side and a pair of long tail spines. Its light, spiny build suggests it swam in open water, probably catching tiny animals, darting away quickly rather than relying on armour.

A jawless armoured fish, an osteostracan about 8 cm long, from the Late Silurian of Saaremaa, Estonia. The head and front half of its body were enclosed in one solid, spindle-shaped box of bone covered with small nipple-like tubercles, with the eyes close together on top and sensory fields along its sides. It had no paired fins, swam slowly with its short scaly tail and sucked up food from the sea floor, relying on its bony armour for protection.

A slender, jawless anaspid fish about 12 cm long from the Late Silurian of Ringerike, Norway. Its torpedo-shaped body was covered in narrow scales, with a long row of small gill openings behind each eye, a crest of hooked scales along the back, long fin folds along the belly and a large, down-turned tail. A fast, agile swimmer, it fed on small particles in the water and on the bottom.

A small, early jawed fish a few centimetres long from the early Silurian of Guizhou, China, about 439 million years ago, one of the oldest jawed vertebrates known from more than scattered scales. It was a spiny relative of the earliest sharks, with sharp spines in front of its fins, a bony shoulder armour and a long row of extra paired spines along its belly. Its spines made it very hard to swallow, while its jaws let it catch small prey.

A straight-shelled nautiloid from mid-Silurian seas of Europe and North America, with a long, slowly tapering shell ringed along its whole length by strong, rounded ridges. Gas-filled chambers kept it afloat while it hunted with a ring of grasping arms and a sharp beak. Its strong, ridged shell protected it from most attackers, and it could jet backwards to escape.

A shrimp-like crustacean up to about 20 cm long including its tail, from the Silurian of Scotland. A smooth, two-sided shell covered its head and front body, and a long, muscular abdomen ended in a dagger-like spine flanked by two shorter ones. By flicking this three-pronged tail it could shoot away from danger very fast; it probably fed on dead and small animals on the sea floor.

A solitary horn coral a few centimetres tall from mid-Silurian reefs of Gotland and England, shaped like an upside-down, four-sided pyramid. Its polyp could close itself in completely with four triangular lid plates that fitted over the square cup like a trapdoor. Fixed in place and catching small prey with its tentacles, it was almost impossible to harm once shut.

A giant sea lily from the very end of the Silurian and the start of the Devonian, found worldwide. Instead of anchoring to the sea floor, its stem, up to a few metres long, ended in a large, chambered bulb that probably worked as a float, so the animal hung upside down from the sea surface with its big, feathery crown of branching arms below. Its huge size and its ability to regrow lost arms made it very hard to kill, though it could barely move.

A planktonic graptolite of the early and mid-Silurian, found worldwide, whose colony was a single long, gently curved branch often 10 cm or more long. Along one side ran a row of small cups, each holding a filter-feeding zooid, with their mouths curled back into hooks. Weak on its own, it drifted in vast numbers and budded new members so fast that it spread across the world's oceans.

A sea snail a few centimetres across from mid-Silurian reefs of Dudley in England and Gotland in Sweden. Its thick, low, almost disc-shaped shell had angular whorls with a strong, knobbly keel around the shoulder and a wide opening underneath. It crept slowly over the reef grazing on microbial films and debris, and could withdraw into its heavy shell, which few predators could crack.

A small millipede from near Stonehaven in Scotland, dated to about 425 million years ago, one of the oldest land animals known. Its body rings carry spiracles, the openings of breathing tubes, the earliest direct evidence of an animal breathing air. It lived among the first low plants beside lakes and fed on rotting plant matter; like living millipedes it could probably curl up inside its hard rings when attacked.

A big crocodile-line predator about 5 to 6 metres long from the Late Triassic of southern Poland, about 205 million years ago, named after the dragon of Kraków legend. It had a huge, deep skull, strong upright legs and two rows of bony scutes down its back. Its fossil droppings are full of crushed bone, so it bit through and swallowed the skeletons of its prey, a habit otherwise known only from tyrannosaurs.

One of the largest land predators of the Early and Middle Triassic, about 245 million years ago in southern Africa, reaching about 5 metres long. Its enormous head made up about a fifth of its length, with long jaws full of big curved teeth, on a bulky body with sturdy half-sprawling legs. One of the first giant archosaur relatives after the end-Permian extinction, it could overpower large plant-eating synapsids, but it was slow and heavy.

A large ichthyosaur about 8.6 metres long from the Middle Triassic seas of Nevada, about 244 million years ago, whose name means 'lizard-eating ruler of the sea'. Its big skull carried large, blade-like teeth with cutting edges front and back, made for slicing up prey rather than just grabbing fish. It was one of the first sea predators able to kill animals as big as itself, including other marine reptiles.

One of the largest phytosaurs, up to about 7 metres long, from the Late Triassic rivers of Arizona about 225 million years ago. It looked much like a giant crocodile, with a long, deep snout full of teeth and thick bony armour on its back, but its nostrils sat on a mound just in front of the eyes instead of at the tip of the snout. It lay in wait in the water and seized fish and animals that came to drink.

One of the largest predatory dinosaurs of the Triassic, about 5 metres long, from Germany about 210 million years ago. It was a lightly built, long-legged relative of Coelophysis, with a long neck, grasping three-fingered hands and possibly a pair of thin crests along its snout. Fast and agile, it could hunt the young of the big plant-eater Plateosaurus, but its slim frame could not take much punishment.

A plant-eating, armoured crocodile-line archosaur about 3.5 metres long from the Late Triassic of the south-western United States, about 215 million years ago. Its body was extraordinarily wide and flat, almost as broad as it was long, and covered by a shield of many rows of interlocking bony plates edged with small hooked spikes. With a small head and a blunt, upturned snout for rooting, it was slow and harmless but almost impossible to bite through.

The largest known relative of mammals that was not itself a mammal: an elephant-sized dicynodont about 4.5 metres long and weighing about 9 tonnes, from Poland about 210 million years ago. Unlike earlier dicynodonts it stood on straight, pillar-like legs, and it cropped plants with a toothless horny beak flanked by two short tusks. Its sheer bulk made it very hard for any predator to bring down.

A turtle-like placodont about 1.3 metres long from the Middle Triassic seas of Switzerland and Italy, about 240 million years ago. Its broad, flat body was covered by a carapace of fused, knobbly bony plates, with a second small shield over the hips, and its mouth held a few huge, flat teeth for crushing shellfish. Slow in the water, it relied on its armour to shrug off attacks.

A turtle with only half a shell, about 40 centimetres long, from the shallow coastal seas of southern China about 220 million years ago. Its belly was already protected by a complete bony plastron, but its back had only broad, flattened ribs, and unlike modern turtles it still had teeth in its jaws and a long tail. The armoured underside shielded it from predators attacking from below as it swam.

A small gliding reptile about 20 centimetres long including its tail, from New Jersey about 220 million years ago. Like the living flying lizard Draco, it had very long ribs sticking out sideways from its body that held up skin wings, letting it glide from tree to tree. It ate insects and was far too small and fragile to fight, escaping instead by launching itself into the air.

One of the oldest pterosaurs, with a wingspan of about 1.2 metres, from the Late Triassic of the Austrian Alps about 210 million years ago. It had a long, stiff tail, jaws with large front fangs and many small multi-cusped teeth behind, and a thin bony crest along the top of its snout. A quick, agile flier, it probably snatched fish and other small prey.

A small, slender relative of crocodiles about 1 metre long, most of it tail, from the Late Triassic of south Wales about 205 million years ago. Unlike its descendants it lived on land, with long, thin, upright legs that made it a fast runner, a small pointed head and a double row of small scutes down its back. It chased insects and lizards, relying on speed rather than strength.

A slender, long-legged plant-eater about 2.3 metres long from the Late Triassic of Poland, about 230 million years ago, a close relative of the first dinosaurs and perhaps an early bird-hipped dinosaur. It walked on four long, thin legs and had a small head on a long neck, with a toothless, beak-like tip to its lower jaw. It probably ate plants and beetles, and escaped danger by running.

A strange tree-climbing reptile about 50 centimetres long from the Late Triassic of Italy and New Mexico, about 210 million years ago. It had a bird-like head on a long neck, a humped back and an enormous claw on the second finger of each hand, probably used to tear open bark and rotten wood for insects. Its long tail ended in a bony hook that helped it grip branches.

An odd marine reptile about 1 metre long from the Early Triassic seas of Hubei, China, about 248 million years ago, a close relative of the ichthyosaurs. Its long, flat, toothless snout and stretchy throat suggest that it gulped and strained small prey from the water, rather like a baleen whale. A double layer of bony plates along its back gave it unusual protection.

A flat, armoured amphibian about 1 metre long that lived on the bottom of Late Triassic lakes and rivers in Germany and Greenland, about 210 million years ago. It had a very broad, short head with small eyes on top, and kept three pairs of feathery external gills throughout its life. Well camouflaged on the bottom, it ambushed passing prey, snapping by lifting its skull rather than dropping its lower jaw.

A large meat-eating cynodont about 1.2 metres long from the Late Triassic of southern Brazil, about 230 million years ago; its name means 'butcher cynodont'. It belonged to the group that gave rise to mammals, with a long, dog-like skull, big canine teeth and long, slender legs. A swift hunter of small animals, it was lightly built and could not take much punishment.
